Fine weather again prevailed on Saturday to the delight of all local bowlers and the greens in the town were well patrothsed. The various competitions in the town are now proceeding briskly and on the Horse and Jockey Green the third round of the Works Association Competition was entered into. Some very good games wore witnessed by the large number of spectators assembled. Probably the most interesting match of the afternoon was the replayed tie between Orford Shed and Rylands who drew with NO each on the previous Saturday. After a very hard fought game the wireworkers enter into the third round by lg points and to-day they meet Howley Tannery whom they will have to concede GO points.

div.head: 011. FORD. SHED V. IZYLANDS_ NO 1.
div.p: 011. FORD. SHED V. IZYLANDS_ NO 1.

The Orford men had an advantage of 35 points in the handicap but there were only three of their men who returned winning cards. The Church-street men gained some very decisive victories and six of the Orfordites were disposed of without having reached a double figure score.

T Humphries (Rylands) made an exceptionally good start against J Roberts and at the 10th end he lea by 11-2. Roberts however, was not to be accounted for so easily and with some good bowling he brought his score to 11 at the 18th end there then being only two points between the players. A single on the next length proved to be Robert's last score aid Humphries won by a trio of points after a very keen game.

A tight gr.me was played between NV Cottam (Rylands) and J Skelhorne and although the wire- worker led 14-3 at the 14th end, when the game finished after thrre more ends he was only three points in front.

Scoring ten points to his opponent H Langley (1131 ands four in 12 ends Bfl Cunningham's chances of victory looked exceedingly rosy but before he could score again Langley had gained a lead of 11-10 at the 17th end. This turned out to be his last score and in 21 ends the Orford man came off the green with a win of 15-11.
The wireworkers thoroughly deserved their victory but they wilt hive a difficult, task on with Howley Tannery to-day.
THIRD _ROUND.
The games in the third -r-o-u-nd. were also full of interest and the first match was between - C.L.O NO 1 ANT) WHITT:CROSS NO 1.
The final was not decided until Monday evening Rnd after a tight game Whitecross won by only seven points

J Gleave (C.L.C.) had indeed very hard lines in his game with W Jones. for after having led from the first to the 19th end he finally lost by the odd point. After having been six points in arrears at the 4th end Jones played a steady game and did well to win by the odd chalk.
H Broadhurst (Whitecross) played a fine game against T Timperley and after having peeled with 5,6, 7,9, 11 and 13 he lost by two points.
-- T Ellison (Whitecross) and J Bibby kept pretty even all through their game and it was only on the last three ends that the Railwayman got in front and he won by 1544 at the 22nd end.
-- T Garnett (C.L.(1.) P 798 in a had way with A Gleave and although both players played neat bowls the White- cross man had a win of 15-1 to his credit.

W Bridge (C.L.C.) played well against A Thornley and the game was very undecided up to the last end. At the 20th end the players peeled with 13 each but on the next length Thornley got a good double and won by two points.
Seven points is not a great win and the railwaymen have given their opponents a good run for their money.

CROSFIELD'S NO. 1 V. LOCKER'S NO. 2. Locker's would indeed have shown poor form if they had not won over Crosfield's, who had to concede them 65 points. Such a lead needs a lot of wins to reduce and the soapery men tried bard but without avail and they eventually lost by 49 points.

If all the Locker's men had played like V Wilson the win would have been a far more de 'hive one, for ha only lost to C Millington by the odd point in 21 ends. Millington was in rare form and got arv..y from the first end only to be checked at the 11th end when Wilson•had a lead of 9-8. After three more ends the Locker's man led 11-9, hut at the 16th end the score was equal with 11 each. Wilson only wanted one point at the 19th end when his opponent wanted three. At the 20th end Millington was only 13-11 behind and with a beautiful double on the next end he won by the odd point.

After having led 10-4 at [the 9th end J Hill (Cron- fields) had all his work cut out to maintain a lead over W Callon until the finish, when he only won by two points. From the 9th to the 18th end Callon scored nine points to his opponent three, the score being equal with 13 each. Two singles on the succeeding ends gave Hill the winning card with 15-13.

A similar game was fought between T Wilson (Locker's) and R Edgington, for the Crosfield's man only lost by two points in 19 ends. In the early part of the game Wilson had a slight advantage, but the Soapery man played well and showed, what be could really do to finish only two points behind the Lockers man.
-- A Webb (Crosfields) played a steady game against D Roberts and after baying led 14-10 at the 20th end he lost on the 2Eh length by one point.

-- On the last series of players Crosflelds gained some very sweeping victories but the last man for Lockers, H Mather, played a hard game with R Brobbin and although he led 14-Bat the 19th end it was not until the 25th length had been run that he won and then only by one point.
CORPORATION V I,TAYLORS. With an advantage of 25 points in the handicap, Naylor's had a pretty easy thing on with the Corpora- tion team, and they finally won by 41 points.

-- There were some heavy losses on either side and there were only about four games which can be turned as tight encounters. -- J Handles really ought to have won over J Howarth (Naylors') for at the 11th end he led by 10-4 but such was Howarth's good form that at the Bth end he peeled with 11. At the 20th end the score was again equal with 13 each and on the next length the Naylor's man gained his winning two points. -- G F Rice (Corporation) and W Taylor put up a good show and peeled with 5, 10, 11,and again at the 20th end the score was 13 each. on the next length the Corpora- tion man gained a single, thus being 14-13 ahead of Taylor who, however, bowled a good pair and landed both, thus winning by the odd one.
-- E Lunt (Naylor's) had no help from the fates for after having led 13-11 at the 19th end he finally lost by the narrow majority of one, the game having extended over 22 ends.
-- The Naylor's men are not down to play to-day, but no doubt they will give their opponents a hot time in the next round.

ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ANGLING ASSOCIATION. (N.A. CENTRE).

I hope the members of the society will let me down lightly for the absence of notes on Saturday last. It was most important business that prevented me sending the usual reports. Last week end, the weather being ideal, a large num- ber of members were out but the results were very poor. Of course the roach now on the board will take a lot of beating, especially from our local waters, the first and second weighing over lib Soz and lib 7oz. Still there are plenty of specials left for Norton and other waters; the cash for roach alone amounts to 27s 6d independent to the set board prizes.
LONG BARN.
I have not beard of —Members doing much at Long Barn though the latest report from there was that the water was in splendid condition.

div.head: CHESTER.
div.p: CHESTER.
The Dee was visited -Wa-v--e-r-v- poor results and the only specimens recorded up to the present are a couple of bream caught by J. Bryers.
HARTFORD. The saver has had more than its fair share of Anglers this season and although they have had good sport now and again not a single specimen has yet been weighed in from here.
NORTON.

A large number of members visited here last week- end. Those who came on Saturday afternoon had the better of those who only arrived on the Sunday morning. There was a lot of rubbish sailing on the top of the water which had a tendency to annoy those who were fishing fine, but in spite of this several had fair bags of fish. The leaders were Messrs Potter, Taylor, Warburton and Singleton. There is not much time in band to beat the roach already weighed in from here for the July special, its weight being lloz 6drs, becsuse the following week-end most of the members will be at the opening match. That gives only this week-end to beat it. Members Pleßse note that they must not go on any land on the off-side with- out first asking permission from the person who rents the laud. The society will not answer for them if they do and their fish will not be allowed to weigh for the prizes. THE OPENING MATCH.

Members who wish to go to the opening match by the motor char-a-banc must enter up their names at once at the club house as there is only room for about six more and those down first must have the privileve of going. The remainder must go by 'bus. There will be a notice put up at headquarters giving the time of starting, Sze. TRENT AND MERSEY CANAL. We have received a notice from the Trent and Mersey Canal Co. that they are letting the water off at different stages and are coming as low down as Preston Brook tunnel on August 6th. This should do our length a great deal of good and no doubt one or two members will be on the scene during operations.

ON HOLIDAY. Just as I was about to post up these notes I have received a letter from one of our members Mr C Ashton, who is on holiday and angling at the same time.— angling at early morning and evenings and pleasure seeking during the day lie is staying at Caistor near Yarmouth where travelling, board and lodgings and private room and all are within reach of most anglers.i As there is fish in abundance, it is a wonder many more ' locals do not take advantage of it. To show what real sport he has had I publish a list of fish taken each day. div.head: CYCLIST'S NOTE-BOOK.
div.p: THE CYCLIST'S NOTE-BOOK.
[By " Silver Street."]
TO THE ISLE OF M.N.

As many cyclists are at present discussing the Isle of Man as a possible scene of a pleasant holiday on the wheel,—and a more charming place can scarcely be found so near to Warrington,— it may not Be amiss to describe the best cycling route to Fleetwood: No money advantage is gained by riding to the more distant port, but one of the most interesting parts of Lancashire is traversed, namely the Pylde, a square patch of land enclosed between the rivers Wyre and Ribble, the sea, and the high road from Preston to Garstang. The way-farer from Warrington comes to two sign-posts at Winwick Church, both indicating Wigan, but no one takes the right hand road twice. Seven miles of the vilest Yorkshire setts is enough for anyone. So the left hand road via Newton will be our choice. Just after leaving Newton, a modest milestone will be noticed on the left hand side of the road. On one side you read Wigan 6, and on the other Warrington 6. Under the tuft of grass behind , this milestone the writer of a tale in " Tit-Bits " hid al lead tube containing a hundred golden sovereigns in the days when the whole country went off its head over the" Hidden treasure" craze. Clues were given in the Thursday morning's issue, and a young clerk started from Manchester and went straight to the hoard the same day. So you won't need to dismount and look for it; just notice the figures on the stone and pass on. Don't chip it either, nor put your initials on, nor an outline of your foot, nor your com- panion's, but leave it alone, there's a dear fellow. Although the whole road to Wigan is paved, yet they are small granites and are very comfortable, and where the tram lines fork, take the right hand road through the centre of the town. At Standish:you are 400 feet up, and keep on the high level through Coppull to Charneck Green (20 miles). At Euxton Junction the road takes a sudden right angle under the railway and as sudden a left right angle on the other side. Then you take the fourth turn on the left to Penwortham Bridge, over the River Ribble, along the Strand-road, and keep straight on over the Marsh to Ashton Brow, where the tramlines appear again, This very easy side road avoids the centre of Preston with its hills and trams altogether. At the Plough Inn there is a choice of roads. Your objective is Great Singleton, 11 miles by either road. The plainest is through Kirkham and Weeton, and if you take that one, just think, as you traverse the five miles of kidney cobbles from Kirkham to Singleton, of the times we cyclists used to enjoy in the SO's and 00's when the Fylde, and in fact, the whole of West Lancashire from Liverpool to Morecambe, was laid with those dear little eggs. And utter an Ave for the souls, living and otherwise, of the cyclists who gradu- ally got them torn up and broken into macadam. flow we wrote to the papers ! How we badgered councillors and turnpike boards before anything was done! And how we suffered on those good old ordinaries and the solid safeties ! _ _ _

Returning to the Plough Inn, a fine bit of typical Lancashire scenery can be enjoyed by taking the right hand road under Lea-road station, and over the canal to Catforth, where the canal is again lurched over by another of those little hump-backed bridges. At I Woodsfold you come across one of the old village greens, so many thousands of which have been filched from the sleepy villagers and railed in with the land- lord's domain. This, however, is a green worth the I name, and at the other side is a fine country public- house, the Derby Aries, Inskip. I hope your pro- gramme suffers you to get a meal there. After that come Elswick, Thistleton and Great Singleton. From there the road keeps more or less parallel with the River Wyre, though we don't see much of it, and don't want to, either, for it is only a mile wide estuary. The old market town of Poulton is out of our way, but in the-market place the stocks and cross or whipping post are very well preserved. Returning to our route at Skippool Bridge some good orchard country is passed,and the railway crossed at Cleveleys Station. Any of the north roads from there will put you in Fleetwood after 5 miles. At Bourn Hall is one of the largest poultry farms in England. The full ride is 51 miles. s PATCHING A LARGE .S. (o:ford-lane). When a hole or slit is to be mended, the most satis- factory repair includes a piece put inside the tube, as well' as a patch outside. The white sulphur deposit round the hole inside is first removed with a wet match head and the dampness taken up with the corner of a rag inserted in the same way. The inner patch must be rolled up and pushed in dry. To use solution before it is inside, and persuaded into its place under the hole is a mistake, and the slit will almost certainly be made bigger. When you have got the patch in its place, insert the nozzle of the tube of solution and squeeze a very little out, rubbing it over the patch. In a few minutes it will be firm, and ready for the outside repair to be completed. Again I give the warning,—never try to put a solutioned piece of rubber inside a tube, and in every case use the least quantity of solution possible. To CORRERPONDENTS.—As I hope to be riding to, in, and from Devonshire for a week or two, will corres- pondents please wait for an answer till my return. WESLEYAN CYCLING CJXB. Saturday afternoon was spent at the .National Children's Home and Orphanage, Frodsham. The Wesley Guilds of the Warrington Circuit had arranged for a garden party to be held there, and about .10 members of the club travelled by cycle. A good pro- gramme of sports had been drawn up, and several prizes were carried off by the cyclists. Tea was served in the large hall, and about 180 sat down, after which a meeting was held when Miss Dutton handed the prizes to the winners. Mr. K. F. Bishop was the chairman and Miss Kershaw and one of the little girls in the home sang. Some good photographs of the large party were obtained by Mr. Bishop. The return journey by Kingsley and Acton Bridge was com- menced at eight o'clock and with the exception of one puncture and a burst tyre, both easily repaired, the return was void of incident, the party reaching the Stag Bridge at 10 o'clock. Lamp time to-night, 9.21 next Saturday, 9.15.

div.head: INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RENA BITES.
div.p: INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RENA BITES.
Opening of a New Branch.

The Executive of the Warrington District No 4 met on Tuesday night in the Primitive Methodist schoolroom, Legh-street for the purpose of instituting a new branch of the order. Bro. .3 J Gee D.P.C.R., was appointed to conduct the ceremony of instituting the new tent, and was assisted by Bro.D Hamlett, D.R.R., Bro. S Fernley, Levire, Bro. 3 Hill, A Sec. and Bro. T Winstanley, D.S. The initiation of 32 new members forming the new adult mixed tent was then preoeeded with, there being 15 female and 17 male members initiated. It was decided that the name of the tent should be "Zion " ; meeting place, Primitive Methodist school- room, Legh-street ; meetings to be held every fourth Tuesday in the month, at 8 p.m. The following officers were then appointed for the new tent :—Bro John Himsworth. C.R. ; Bro H Jones, D.R. ; Sister Elsie Jones, P.C.R. ; Bro Frank Shaw, Levite ; Sister Gertrude Abbotts, guardian ; Bro B T Parkes, secre- tory ; Sister Florence Wadsworth, minute secretary ; Bro Albert Spruce, treasurer ; Bro Fred Shaw, steward. Bro J J GEE and Bro W WRI GHT afterwards addressed the new members and officers of the tent on the work of the Order and opportunities of extension. under the National Insurance Act.

The new tent opened in Bank Quay Mission Thewlis- street, on Saturday, July 6th, continues its usefulness by initiating new members, and extending the order. Arrangements are being made for new branches to be opened next week, at the Independent Methodist Schoolroom, Stockton Heath, and a female branch at Brick-street Mission, Warrington. At the Executive meeting it was decided to send a donation of 5 guineas to the women and children's fund (innocent victims of the transport strike, London). Sunday school teachers and leaders of churches desirous of forming branches of the order, are requested to call or communicate with Mr. Fernley, 71, Bridge-st.
GOLF.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION.
Date of Next Season's Final Tie.

At a meeting of the Northern Union League com- mittee, held at Huddersfield on Tuesday, the league final tie was fixed for May 2rd next. The Morecambe club was elected to membership in the new Yorkshire and Lancashire Combination. The official list of league referees elected by the clubs showed that the only new name was that of Mr D Longbottom, Halifax. John Harrison, a York player appealed to the com- mittee to have his name struck off the York register, in accordance with a promise made by the York secretary when he signed on for that club. After hearing the evidence of witness, the committee granted his request

It was announced by LIBERALS AND Mr. ASQUITH on Tues- THE NAVY. day that the Navy Votes will come up in the House of Commons on Monday. Here will present itself the occasion of a great battle between parties with widely diverging views as to what it is necessary for us to do and to keep on doing to maintain our supremacy at sea. The divergencies, it needs to be pointed out, are not on strictly party lines. On a broad view it might be said that the demand for extravagant expenditure comes from the Opposition, and that all the members of Parliament in favour of a non-provocative policy are to be found on the Ministerial benches, That sweeping division would almost abso- lutely represent the facts of the case in a' sweeping sort of way. But it must not be supposed that all the supporters of the Government are on the side of restraint in naval expenditure. Indeed, the contrary is the case, It is absurd beyond measure to speak of the Ministerialists as "the Little Navy" party. There are few severe economists of the older type in the House of Commons to-day. The cry for retrenchment is, in fact, hardly raised at all. The Liberal Party is in entire agreement with the standard of naval strength which has been. set up by the present Government, and set up, as we may justly claim, for the first time. Where differences arise on the Liberal side, I they are, in respect of expenditure, in excess of that required for maintaining the standard of naval armament equalling that of the next two strongest Powers, with ten per cent. over.

Mr. Churchill is expected on Monday, or very early in the debate on the Naval Vote, to make a statement of great and even thrill- ing importance. That is as it may be. The First Lord:of the Admiralty is at the moment the object of keen speculation. Since he went to Whitehall he has seemed to some of those who have been closely watching his career to have become a new man. It must be ad- mitted that his own circumstances have vastly changed. He is no longer the bete noir of the Tory Party, and on the Liberal side there is a story afloat to which we do not attach too much importance, that his extensive ideas of expenditure on the Navy have brought him into con- flict with Mr. LLOYD GEORGE. We can very well wait until next Monday (and a few days longer if necessary) to learn from his own lips what view he takes of present and future necessities. Rumours of Cabinet dissensions are quite clearly the invention of the enemy. There is probability in a forecast which appeared on Tuesday night as to the First Lord's intention. It is said that he will propose the appointment of a Commission, of which LORD FISHER will be chairman, con- sisting of experts in special departments of the public service, for the purpose of investigating certain naval affairs. There can never be any objection to inquiry by competent men, and, if an inquiry is to take place, it is obviously wrong to credit Mr. CHURCHILL with large proposals for additional expenditure in advance of anything that the commission of experts may say. Another exceedingly probable statement is to the effect that the First Lord will make proposals as to an increase—not a large increase, perhaps, but something not quite negligible—in the pay of the men. This is a naval reform that has undoubtedly been long delayed. It is an open secret that there is much discontent on the lower deck arising ' out of the low rates of pay and other griev- ances. Members of Parliament heard much of this when they were down with the fleet the other day. One Petty Officer said to a representative of our own staff that a rise in wages would produce such a new spirit among the men as would be equivalent to another Dreadnought. This is a graphic, and perhaps an extravagant way of stating the case. But it cannot be doubted that the discontent on the lower-deck is something that cannot be much longer ignored, and that a generous manner of dealing with it would lin many ways be well repaid. Probably this is one of the principal of the many subjects with which a Royal Commission would be expected to deal.

The congratulations of MILLION PENNY every inhabitant of FUND COMPLETE. Warrington are jointly ithe due of the organisers of the Infirmary Million Penny Fund and the promoters of the Old English Fair held last week. For the last few years stupendous efforts have been put forth in eve/ y direction to gather together the million pennies which were to place the Infirmary on a sound financial footing, and at last the task is accomplished I The £4,166 13s. 4d., which is the sum total of so much copper, has been obtained, and there is even a surplus. There is no question that the effort would have been heart-breaking but for the substantial help afforded by the two great fairs held in Victoria Park. These money-raising enterprises have both succeeded beyond the bounds of the rosiest anticipations. No less a sum than £1,380 was gleaned by the gallant voluntary showmen last week, and as only £541 was required to clear off the fund, the cup is full to overflowing. probably £9OO profit will accrue from the venture which was so lavishly blessed by the weather

and public patronage last week. The men who have done so much—and with such remarkable perseverance and courage—for a great public Institution are to be envied the feelings of satisfaction,in a task nobly accom- plished which must be paramount in their hearts and minds to-day. Again we say "All credit to them 1"
Mr. F. E. Smith has tlia F. E.'s opportunity of his life. OPPORTUNITY. On Friday last he

accused Mr. Devlin of "betraying Ulster." Mr. Devlin has now offered to resign his seat and contest it against Mr.F.E. Smith, fighting in Protestant Belfast for the great twin causes of Protestantism and Tariff "Reform." Mr. Smith can scarcely refuse (says the " Daily News") without tacitly avowing his con- viction that some thousands of Ulstermen, at any rate, like being 'betrayed" by Mr. Devlin—or at least prefer it to being repre- sented by Mr. Smith.
The Insurance Act has THE ACT. come into operation,and

the nation has received it, according to the "Times," with " apathetic acquiescence." If a considerable section of the Tory Press has not been exaggerating enormously, it must have been bitterly dis- appointed that the occasion was not cele- brated by spontaneous demonstrations of indignant householders all over the kingdom displaying home-made banners from their windows inscribed with the brave device— "We won't lick stamps." But in spite of the " Times," the attitude of the nation to the Insurance Act could not possibly be gauged by watching the faces of the people in the street on Monday, and attempting to read their indignation apathy, or enthusiasm. A much more practical test was afforded by the by-election at Hanley, where a Tory leaflet was circu- lated which told the workingman voter that Saturday would be the last day on which he would receive his wages intact. That appeal to the inherent dislike of average human nature for any legislation which takes money out of its pocket was quite powerless to pre- vent a Liberal victory, even though the Progressive vote had been split by a Liberal and a Labour candidate being in the field at the same time.

There can be little HISTORY REPEATING doubt that the experi- ITSELF. ence of the Tory party with Old Age Pensions is repeating itself, nzutatis mutandis, with the National Insurance Act. The Tory party attacked the Liberal Old Age Pension scheme because it was non-contributory, and it was a very short time indeed after the passing of the Act before Tory members were ready to complain of slander if it was suggested that they had been opposed to it. The majority of Tories could not resist the temptation of making capital out of the mis- understandings, misrepresentations, and temporary unpopularity to which the National Insurance scheme was exposed because it was contributory. Already the "Observer "is cautioning the Party to which it plays the part of "Sir Oracle," that the endeavour to score a brief electioneering advantage by running down the Insurance Act may be very indiscreet.
Last week it was "MANY gravely asserted, on INVENTIONS." so-called good authority

that tile National Insurance CoMmissioners' Department was in state of hopeless confusion. That authori- tative information was not sturdy enough to survive over the week-end. But the enemies of the National Insurance Scheme still clung desperately to the "invention" that the sanatorium benefits which the Act promised were not forthcoming. And they were wonderfully cheerful over what was said to be a Liverpool dock strike against the Act. The outcry over the sanatoria was as veritable a mare's nest as the anti- Insurance campaign has yet been able to discover. The money for the sanatoria has been voted; the cash is in bank, waiting. But the system must be developed carefully, as necessity and experience guides. The attack from this side is based on the absurd assumption that hundreds of thousands of insured persons will develop consumption in the first week. The Liverpool strike against the Insurance Act was nothing of the kind. It was a strike against the united efforts of employers and trade union leaders to decasualise dock labour by the establishment of a new clearing-house system.

The return of Mr. R. L. THE LIBERAL Outhwaite at Hanley, TRIUMPH AT an Saturday, by the HANLEY. substantial majority of 654, coupled with the poor poll of the Labour nominee, ought to have a steadying influence in politics, and should teach the extremists of the Labour party a severe lesson. The figures were as follow :
R. L. Outhwaite (L) G. H. Rittner (C) S. Finney (Lab) 1,694

Lib. majority over C0n.... 654 9 ~Lab.... 4,953 99 At the last election the late Mr. Enoch Edwards, M.P., standing' as Liberal-Labour candidate, had a mejority of 3,683 ; but in 1900, in a straight fight, the Conservative beat Mr. Edwards by 642, and at the previous election in 1895, the Liberal majority was only 285. The poll on Saturday, after one of the most strenuous contests on record, shows clearly that Hanley is predominatingly Liberal, and that although Mr. Edwards was regarded as a Labour member, he owed his position to Liberal votes, and to his general support of Liberalism.

div.head: WORKING THE INSURANCE ACT.
div.p: WORKING THE INSURANCE ACT.

Not only as a busy industrial town but as an import- ant centre for the administration of the Act,Warrington has experienced its full share of the work involved by such an innovation as the far-reaching health scheme which the Government has brought into operation this week. The obtaining of insurance cards, stamps and books, has occupied the attention of employers and employed alike, but now that the mutual step has been taken everything will doubtless work smoothly and efficiently. The Divisional Office in Bridge-street, from which the whole of the books for Lancashire and Cheshire are issued, presents a scene of much activity. The offices are situated in the premises formerly occupied by Messrs. J. M. Greenhalgh and Co., and a staff of about 100 persons—some temporary, some per- manent —is engaged. Since tho 14th ult, no fewer than 200,000 unemployment books—emergency, temporary, &c.—have been issued. Mr Williams is the Divisional Officer, and Mr Mellor the insurance officer. The Labour P achange in Winmarleigh-street is, of course, concerned with the working of the employment section of the Act. The staff has been augmented by the appointment of four temporary clerks. Since the Ist June over 5,000 unemployment application forms have been issued. The Post Office officials also play an important part in working the measure. No additional assistance has been procured at Warrington and the extra work has been met by a proportionate increase in the hours of attendance. Over 2,000 deposit contributors' cards have been sent out. Employers have to obtain their stamps from the Post Office and about £1.5,000 worth have been received already.

In returning thanks, Mr. LAWRANCE said he and Ins future wife would do their best to elevate the lives and improve the characters of the children committed to their charge and their duties would be carried out with zeal and fidelity. Mr. Lawrance, who is 33 years of age, has for the past seven and a half years been headmaster of the Bolton and County of Lancaster Certified Industrial School. Previously he was master in charge of the lower school of St. Luke's Boys' School, Chelsea. The institution at Bolton is a farm school, accomodat- ing 200 boys, and the industries carried on for the training of the pupils include farming, gardening, shoe making, tailoring and joinery. There is also a military band. The boys are taught horticulture and swimming, and Mr. Lawrence has taken a great interest in their out-of-school life, organising their games and field sports. He has a thorough knowledge of the domestic routine and general management of a well-ordered institution, and has been accustomed to control a large staff of cfficers. Miss Hart began her Poor Law experience as matron's assistant in the Reigate Union, having previously held a position of housekeeper, in which she had the superintendence of a sewing room where needlework was carried on in all its branches. She is now assistant matron at the Warren Farm School, Brighton, where 300 children are in residence. The ,1 girls are all trained in housewifery, and Miss Hart has the general supervision of the work.

div.head: PADGATE COTTAGE HOMES.
div.p: PADGATE COTTAGE HOMES.
The New Superintendent and Matron.

Mr. Charles Edwin Lawrence, of Bolton, has been appointed superintendent and schoolmaster, and Miss Alice Ethel Hart, of Brighton, matron of the Cottage Homes, Padgate. The appointments are joint, the successful candidates having arranged to be married before taking up their duties a month hence. The salaries are :ClOO per annum for the master and superintendent and £4O per annum for the matron, with apartments, rations ana the usual allowances. The appointments were made at the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday. The Schools Committee at their meeting on July sth considered 72 applications for the joint appoint- ments. Eight candidates were selected to appear before the committee on July 10th when it was recommended that the following candidates be requested to attend the Board meeting viz :—Mr John W Box, 331, Walton-Breck-road, A nfield, Liver- pool and Miss Annie Spence, 10, Powell-street, Latchford; Mr and Mrs Fred Johnson, St Chad's View Winsford ; Mr Charles Edwin Lawrance, Bolton and County Industrial School, Lostock Junction, Bolton, and Miss Alice Ethel Hart, Warren Farm Schools, Brighton. The selected candidates having been interviewed by the Board, the choice fell upon Mr. Lowrance and Miss Hart who were unanimously appointed.
ALICE E. H. (Matron.)

div.head: WARRINGTON CANINE SOCIETY. ---- EIGHTH LOCAL SHOW.
div.p: WARRINGTON CANINE SOCIETY. ---- EIGHTH LOCAL SHOW.

The Warrington arid District Canine Society is entitled to congratmlate itself upon the success of its eighth local show which was held in the Assembly Rooms, Conservative Club, on Thursday evening. Although the number of entries-125 -was slightly below last year's, there was a striking improvement in quality, which was especially noticeable in the retriever and terrier classes. Mr V V Davies, of Stockton Heath one of the best known breeders of retrievers in the north of England, carried off all the honours in that class. His record was five first, five second and four third prizes. Mrs. Pennington' of Newton-le-Willows, was another prominent winnerand in the pomeranian or pomeranian miniature she secured an easy first with her two-year- old Woodhead Caocolite Mite which weighs 311 b. and has only made one previous appearance in the show ring. Mr Tom Lawson, of Glossop, was the judge and competition was so keen that his task was a somewhat difficult one. Mr FIV White discharged the duties of hon. secretary with diligence and tact and Mr F W Wareing was quite at home as show manager. div.head: SPLENDID RESULT OF OLD ENGLISH
div.p: SPLENDID RESULT OF OLD ENGLISH
FAIR.

The Million Penny Fund is now comple,e—such is the gratifying result of the Old English Fair held in Victoria Pars last week. The magnificent weather and the unique round of attractions (-flew all Warring- ton tr. the fair on Seturday and the takings far eiceeded all previous records. Tim gross receipts were as follows : s. d. Tbursdey Friday • 375 5 4 Saturday 640 7 9 Cash received since • 24 17 0

It is impossible to state as yet, what the nez pro- ceeds will be, but it would probably be safe to estimate them at about z,:.000. One thing is certain Toe object of the prornotors —to c,anplete the Million Penny Fund—has been achieved, and there will als., be a handsome surplus. Saturday was a day of unalloyed gaiety at Victoria Park, and all the shows did a towing laiFi.,ess. The cr.mds grew larger as the day advanced, and never has the spacious park been so densely thronged as it was between the Inar s of 7 and 1030 on Saturday evening. The voluntiry assistants who manned the roundabouts, electric cars, &c.. worked herolcally to keep pace witli the hosts of patrons who sttupgled for places, and the scene was most animated and not without ex3iterrient. It was no doubt with feelings of relief that the harasFel th ugh ever-cheerful workers hailed "closing time " RESULTS OF COMPETITIONS. •

The following won the prizes in the gnessing competition : —Reginald Brown, 86, Church-street, Philip Jenkinson, 33. div.head: SATURDAY'S OPENING CEREMONY.
div.p: SATURDAY'S OPENING CEREMONY.

Mrs. Ziba Armitage opened the fair on Saturday afternoon, in the presence of a large attendance. Mr. J. H. SMETHURST (chairman of the Board of Management of the Infirmary and chairman and founder of the Million Penny Fund) presided. He said Pis first words were of thankfulness to Almighty God for the splendid weather He had seen fit to give them. The committee were extremely grateful for the support accorded to them by the people of Warrington and they hoped that day would mark a record in their proceedings, and that they would have cause for thankfulness that the fund had been completed. (Applause). On Thursday the gross proceeds were S-339 15s. 5d., on Friday £375 ss. 4d., and it was for the people who attended that clay to see to it that they had at least SZOO more to their credit. (Applause). He was very optimistic on that point, and thought there was no doubt they would obtain the amount. (Applause): Mrs. Armitage, who was to open the fete, was the president of the Ladies' Committee of the Infirmary, and had done splendid work for the institution. For thirty years she had been connected with it in an official capacity, and they would understand the enormous amount of interest she took in it. He wished they had more ladies like Mrs. Armitage, who were willing to help them as she did. (Applause). Mrs ARMITAGE said she was not present in her private capacity but as president of the Ladies' Com- mittee of the infirmary. Perhaps it was suitable that that committee should be represented at the fair. (Applause.) Sometimes the committee had a great deal of work to do, and sometimes they had not much, but very often when they wanted to do things they were told that there was no money and they must draw in. For instance, they had not been able to decorate the upper part of the Nurses' Home ; the walla were just as bare as the builders left them three or four years ago. That showed bow much they needed funds (Hear, hear.) She had much pleasure in declaring the fete open and hoped it would be a complete success. (Applause). Mr. F. Simla, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mrs. Armitage, said she took a very deep interest in the welfare of Warrington generally, and of the Infirmary in particular. As president of the Ladies' Committee she had the opportunity of doing a great deal for the benefit of the patients by voicing their requests in the proper quarter. Major APPLETON seconded and the vote was heartily passed. Mr. J. W. WE LSBY then presented bound copies of the programme to Mrs. Armitage and the Chairman. Tee CIT ORMAN thanked Mr. NV elsby for the enormous amount of Work he had done for the Fair as secretary of the Printing and Advertising Committee. Without Mr. Welsby's help in that department, they would have been absolutely "floored," but instead the arrangements were absolutely perfect. (Applause). A vote of thanks to the Chairman was proposed by Mr. ROGER C.TARR, who said, that, as treasurer of the Infirmary he was, perhaps, much more interested than anyone else in the success of the Fair. They owed a deep debt of gratitude to Mr. Smethurst for the work he had done for the Infirmary. (Applause). Mr. ARXIITA GE seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimously.

THANKS. The Committee wish to place on record their hearty thanks for the following special services :---To Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., for motor car for cash staff ; Messrs Peter Walker and Sons, Ltd. for fitting up bar and beer garden, lending utensils for bar, fitting up doll show, band stands, and shop in Bridge-street, and providing bunting ; Messrs Greenall, Whitley and Co., Ltd., utensils for bar; all workers for the Million Penny Fund Committee; Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee (per Alderman Bolton, chairman) for the use of the Park ; Messrs Rylands Bros., Ltd.. for fitting electric light in the Pierrot tent; Manchester Ship Canal Co..for use of ferry boata;Mr .1- A Parfitt,for use of electric launch; voluntary assistants in the bar; Messrs Caldwell for utensils; all donors of goods for the

The annual bowling main for the Crosfield Cup was held at the Liberal Club on Saturday last, and as usual proved a highly popular event. There was a large entry, and the green being in fine condition, some good bowling was witnessed. The games were of a very exciting nature, and the final wale between A Webb and F Walter (secretary of the club) was indeed a keen one. Webb led up to the Bth end when, however, Walker drew the block and ran out the winner by 15-8 amidst the applause of tbe large number of spectators assemblsd. The other prize-winners were :—A Webb, B Forster, Harry Daintitb, 3 T Smith, C Algie, 17 Dale and P Delaney.—Mr Walker received the cup, whic his a massive silver one, and a gold medal, whilst the runner-up (A Webb) received a gold medal. Various other prizes were also given by Councillor 3 T Locker, who, in making the presentations,expressed his pleasure at being there to witness such a splendid Achievement by the winner, in addition to the many other interesting games. (Applause).

LADIES' MAIN AT THE CEMETERY HOTEL. The fine old game of bowls of which Sir Walter Raleigh wee so fond is no longer a favourite sport of man alone, for year after year increased interest is taken in the game by large numbers of the gentler sex. The craze for ladies' mains is rapidly spreading in Warrington and whereas a year or two ago there were only one or two of these choice events there are now several, and one crf the most popular is the annual laiies' main at the Cemetery Hotel, which this year took place on Thursday, the competition being the ninth of its kind under such auspices. The com- mittee cf the Cemetery Bowling Club have all the arrangements in hand and it speaks well for their excellent management that the main in which (;(3 competitors took part was cart ied through without a hitch. The green which was crowded with spectators is in the hest of condition and the quality of the play of many of the ladies was excellent and not a few of them would give some men a severe trouncing. Mr. Willett acted as referee and he was ably assisted by a body of the committee who acted as stewards. The weather was beautifully fine and during the afternoon Messrs. Crosfields' Band played selections of the latest music to the delight of all. The games were keenly contested and the main was continued in the evening tea being served in the hotel. The first prize was a gold watch given by Mr. H. Mather and was won by Mrs. B. Tilling whose game with Mrs. Penniugton who came second was a very exciting one. . Other prize winners were : 3 Mrs Allison, 4 Mrs Bennion, Mrs John Wood, Mrs Bothwell, Miss Tickle, Mrs Cook, Mrs Wilcox, Mrs Milner, Mrs A Scott, Mrs Sunderland, Mrs Crusham, Mrs Bolton, Miss E Gleave, Mrs Gatley, Miss Baldwin, Mrs Kay, Mrs Brooks, Mrs F Dale, Mrs Berry, Mrs W Bridge, Mrs Povey, Mrs Hawtli3roe, Mrs Belford, Miss M Jones, Mrs Ferguson, Mrs Percival, Miss J Weave, Mrs Palmer, Mrs T Bridge Mrs Ford. For those who were knocked out in the firsfround a consolation competition was held and resulted as follows : 1 Mrs Whittle, 2 Mrs Garnett,3 Miss Baldwin 4 Mrs Cleaver, Miss Clarke, Mrs Howarth, Mrs Roberts, Mrs Williams, Miss A Willett, Mrs Belli% Mrs Willett, Mrs H Melbourne, Mrs Robinson, Miss Higham, Mrs S Dale, Mrs A J Jones. Everyone regretted the absence of the president of the club, Mr All Crosfleld who, along with his wife, should have come down to make the presentations but could not owing w unforseen circumstances. However, this duty was ably performed by Mr Willett, who bad a word of congratulation for all the .vinners. After- wards the party adjourned to the billiard room of the hotel where as pleasant social evening was spent. _
Dr. Meredith Young, the Cheshire Medical Officer of Health, attributes the declining birth-rate to the high cost of living, which is bearing most heavily on the middle classes.

div.head: SMOKE.
div.p: SMOKE.
THE MAYOR'S MISTAKEN ATTITUDE.
OUR CORRESPONDENT RETURNS TO THE ATTACK.

[To THE EDITOR " ExAmINER." Sir,—lt is unfortunate his Worship the Mayor should introduce in his replies to any legitimate criticism, an amount of personal feeling which tends to create an atmosphere which makes any reasonable consideration of public questions very difficult. Public men must expect their utterances and actions to be freely discussed and Doctor Joseph cannot claim special exemption. lam quite willing to leave to the judgment of your readers whether my criticism, or as the Mayor pleases to call it, my " attack " was "virulent, unwarranted, and unwarrantable." Doctor Joseph seems to have taken grave personal offence because I treated him as an apologist for, and defender of the Smoke Nuisance. If lam wrong in this the Mayor is alone to blame. In speaking on the question a few months ago Dr. Joseph said :

"There has been a g rod 'deal of claptrap and nonsense spoken about smoke. No medical author- ity had ever yet proved that smoke killed any human being. Noxious vapours might kill persons, but it was never proved beyond dispute that smoke was a nuisance absolutely dangerous to health. Smoke was far from arsthetic and pleasant, it obscured the sun temporarily and the stars also, if one desired t r gaze at them. But as long as people had to live there must be trades, and the question was largely an economic one. When science devised some reasonable means of utilizing smoke, that means would be established, but under present conditions the balance of evidence was in favour of smoke as
against any drastic method of sharing it, so long &sit ass kept within the least possible bounds." This statement is typical of Dr. Joseph's attitude and utterances on the smoke question.

"No medical authority has ever yet proved that smoke killed any human being." We would ask the Mayor is this the way in which his own profession approaches • the problems of sanitation? It would be just as sensible to say of the majority of nuisances our own sanitary authorities have to ueal with "that no medical authority has ever yet proved that they have killed any human being "—for instance overcrowded houses, insufficiently ventilated rooms, dirty dwell- ings, defective pail-closets and ashpits, dirty walls of passages, and all the rest of the 2,000 nuisances which our Health Com- mittee last year insisted upon being remedied. The question with these, as with the smoke nuisance, is not whether they immediately kill, but rather whether they lower vitality and make individuals less capable of combating the evils which tend to kill. The Mayor would not suggest that the activities of the Health Committee be relaxed because the various nuisances it strives to abolish do not directly kill. He would not have us wait till someone was smothered before insisting on properly venti- lated houses. My difference with Dr. Joseph is that he seems to consider the smoke nuis- ance objectionable only or mainly because it is not xsthetic and obscures temporarily the sun and stars, and that objections on the ground of health are largely "clap-trap and nonsense." If this is not the Mayor's position then w hat is ?

Granted "He had never recommended smoke as an absolute benefit " ; but he says, "they ought to make the best of it under existing circumstances without damaging trade." This justifies my criticism, he makes the best of it in every possible way, or to quote what I said, he appears to go out of his way to find excuses for the nuisance. Referring again to above quotation he speaks of "science devising some reasonable means of utilizing smoke." The Mayor takes for granted (and here we come to the crux of the difference between us) that black smoke cannot be burnt in furnace fires so as to increase the efficiency of the boiler, and therefore must be sent into the air. Upon this point I join issue and claim that me- chanical engineering has already solved the problem of black smoke prevention,arid proved beyond question all black smoke to be waste fuel, fuel that can be utilized for the genera- tion of power in ordinary boilers. The only point so far not satisfactorily solved, is how to generate the intense heat required for smelting and annealing metals without the production of a certain amount of black smoke. The law rightly admits of exemp- tion in these particular processes, but only when a manufacturer can prove that, with- out present knowledge, the necessary heat for his process cannot be generated without black smoke. But it is up to the manufac- turer to prove this and many authorities, Warrington I believe included, have been negligent and have scheduled as outside their purview, phimneys of works in which any of these processes are going on. Apart from special trades it is recognized that insmall plants where mechanical stokers would be a heavy charge, liberty is given for the emission of black smoke when hand stoking,for so many minutes to the half hour. In all towns that are in any way progressive the limit is from 2 to 3 minutes in the aggregate to the half hour. Warrington has adopted an extreme limit of 5 rhinutes ; in Oldham about which Mrs. Higgs writes, the limit is 2 minutes. Although Oldham is the centre of a densely populated manufac- turing district getting smoke from surround- ing towns, and although in late years the power required has been increased by a third, still the smoke has been appreciably decreased. An increase of the trade in the town is proof that a fair and firm administration of the powers of the authorities has, instead of handicapping trade, helped to increase it. The result is benefit to the community and saving to the manufacturers. It is quite possible in a comparison of the two towns Oldham would still be the smokier, but the important difference is that in Oldham they do their best to diminish it by a reasonable time limit, while in Warrington a practically ineffective time limit is adopted. I fully appreciate the manufacturers' diffi- culties in controlling black smoke, but these do not arise out of any imposssibility of control, or absence of knowledge, but from subordinate causes such as space, outlay, &c. Apart from the fusing of metalsithe economic control of black smoke is already a solved problem, as manufacturers in our own town and elsewhere have demonstrated. We all admit that reasonable time must be given to manufacturers to put their plant in order, but granting this we claim that the authori- ties, in whose hands the health, cleanliness, and well-being of the town are placed, should exercise, without fear or favour, a steady consistent pressure. with legal compulsion if need be, upon indifferent manufacturers. Where I think the Warrington authorities are at fault is, first, they have accepted the Mayor's false idea that mechanical "science has not yet devised reasonable means to utilize the smoke" ; second, they have adopted an unnecessarily lengthy time limit, in excess of all progressive towns; third, they have shown a timid hesitancy in enforc- ing, where necessary, this excessive limit;

fourth, they have failed to exercise effective supervision over those manufacturers who, may or may not be able to show that they cannot successfully carry on some of their processes without black smoke emission; an 3 fifth, instead of treating criticisms as aa evidence on the part id. the inhabitants of a wish to improve the conditions of life in the town, they have met these criticisms in a personal, petulant spirit. The Mayor, Council and officials of War- rington, would be wise to realise that this desire for a cleaner and healthier town is evidence of a worthy civic spirit,and as such, should be welcomed instead of resented. The longing of the people for a fuller and a better life, for cleaner homes, brighter skies, purer air, and healthier conditions, should be encouraged, not suppressed.—Yours &c, DAYLIGEfT.

Smoke• Pointers. It is interesting to note the attitude of manufacturers when it is in the interests of their industries to control their own smoke. In Nottingham for example where much fine lace is made which is deteriorated by black smoke specks, the manufacturers themselves have solved all difficulties, and have got a special Act of Parliament by which the authorities dominate and rigorously restrain those manpfacturers not specially interested in lace making. Here there is no silly talk about "the more smoke the better for trade," no ignorant assertion "that manufacturers cannot, if they will, control smoke emission," no contention that "science has not devised means of utilizing smoke." When manu- facturers find it to be in their own interest they solve the problem, but when called upon to do it in the interest of the community they say it cannot be done and that their trade must not be hampered. * .x. * Professor 0. N. Witt, in his address to the International Congress of Applied Chemistry held in London in May, 1909, said: "There was a time both in England and on the Con- tinent when smoke was considered a neces- sary evil and had to be suffered. After a while smoke began to be looked upon as a nuisance, and war was declared against it by those who suffered from its disagreeable properties ; but now we know that smoke is waste and that nobody has better cause to wage war against it than he who produces it, * * * The Plaint of a Sanitary Inspector ! "Every inspector was trying to carry out this Act, but the probability was that if an inspector pitted himself against a powerful firm he stood a good chance of getting notice to quit."

n Mr Beilby in his evidence before the Royal Commission on the coal supply stated that, "through inefficient methods of burning coal, something like 60 million tons were wasted annually in the United Kingdom."

div.head: GOLBORNE STREET BAPTISTS. Successful Garden Fete and Sale.
div.p: GOLBORNE STREET BAPTISTS. Successful Garden Fete and Sale.

Given favourable weather a garden fete and open-air sale of work is always a popular event, but of fresco functions have additional attractions during a spell of tropical weather, when to be crowded in a room amidst all the bustle of a sale of work would be almost unbearable. However, a great deal depends upon the spot chosen for the carrying into effect of the enterprise, and if all organisers of such events were as fortunate in securing a site as beautiful as that placed at the disposal of the Golborne-street Baptist Church on Thursday, they would have just cause to be grateful. The object of the function was to augment the church and building funds and, ever willing to help a worthy cause in connection with his church. Mr. Benjamin Few had kindly offered the grounds of Laburnum House, Grappenhall, as a suitable place in which to hold the pleasurable affair. Needless to say the offer was gladly accepted, and a most enjoyable afternoon was spent. A large marquee had been erected, in addition to numerous side shows, in an adjoining field kindly lent by Mr. Millard, and it was here that the chief business of the day was conducted. For those who were inclined t) indulge in games, various corn- petetions, bowling and croquet on the beautiful lawn were additional attractions. A good-toned grama- phone played selections from the operas and other musical tit-bits, to the delight of all. Teas were also provided, and altogether a most enjoyable afternoon was spent by the 250 persons who assembled. The opening ceremony was performed by Mrs Ziba Armitage with Mrs Cantain Savage in the chair. The Rev. J. S. Cbedburn offered prayer. The Rev, H. Ogden, in the course of an explanatory address, said they at Gol borne-street were in the throes of s great deal of change. Their premises looked more like a builder's yard than a church and he did not suppose the outward appearance offered much attraction to new corners. (Laughter.) He wanted as pastor to pay a tribute to the church at Gol borne- street. Although not a large church numerically, the people who attended gave royally and regally. Part of the worship and devotion to God was giving. He failed to see how any individual could worship God without giving his ratio of the goods with which God had endowed bin]. He war not going to say anything about the old school—(hear, hear and laughter)—it belonged to the past—(hear, hear)—and for it there was no hope of resurrection. (Laughter). Part of that effort that afternoon was to relieve the finances of the church, but they wanted a substantial balance over to go to the building funds so that when the scheme was completed they would not be harrasied by the incubus of a fearful debt. They were also there to foster a good feeling of fellowship amongst their own people and those who came to visit them. (Applause). Mrs Armitage, in declaring the fete open, said they knew Co ngregationalista were very like Baptists. (Hear, hear). She thought there was only one point between them. (Hear, hear). (A voice: more water) (laughter.) It was almost like helping a sister church to come and help the Baptists. (Applause.) She was glad also to come to Latchford where she bad resided for 21 years, although her home was in another place now. (Applause.) They, the Baptists, wanted money and she was sure their church needed it, and that old school, really ! (Laughter.) She had been past the church and saw they were putting a new porch in front. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion she hoped they would he extremely comfortable in their new premises and that the good work which had been done in the past would be carried on for the same Lord and Master Whom they all served. (Applause). Mr E Wynne Jones, in proposing a comprehensive vote of thanks, said they all knew what an important part Mr and sirs Armitage had taken in the life of our town from time to time. They were always ready to help a good cause. On behalf of the ollicers of the church he would like to bear testimony to the great service rendered by all who had helped in the prepara- tion of that sale. They were grateful to Mr and Mrs Few for giving them the opportunity for meeting there that afternoon. (Hear, hear). The Rev W Reid in seconding, said he did not know any town like Warrington where such a good feeling existed between the various denominations and he thought it was becoming an increasing quantity in the town. It was very largely owing to the great feeling of fellowship which obtained between them as denominations that the churches were showing such marked signs of increased life. (Hear, hear.) There was no room for jealousy or envious feelings. (Hear, hear.) He was convinced that the one Church of Jesus Christ was making headway in the town and if the good feeling of fellowship was always prevalent the Church could not do other than succeed. They should all sympathise with each other and shpw that sympathy in a practical and Christ-like manner. (Applause). The vote was heartily carried. Mrs Few,Mrs Armitage and Mrs Savage each received a beautiful bouquet from the hands of the Misses Evelyn Pepper, Olive Bamford and Beatrice Jones. The proceeds amounted to about £5O.

On Tuesday Mr. Baker was able to announce in the House of Commons on behalf of the War Office, that the Territorial Force was never so strong as at the present moment, in spite of the efforts of National Service advocates to " crab " it. But Mr. Arthur Lee demanded the Swiss system of universal military service, with a correspon- ding addition to the Army Estimates. Taxes on bread and meat, and conscription, under whatever name it masquerades, are not pro— posals which the working man is likely to swallow with avidity.

div.head: TRIED TO STRANGLE HIS WIFE.
div.p: TRIED TO STRANGLE HIS WIFE.

At the Borough Police Court on Wednesday, John Rigby, Kuutsford-road, was summoned by his wife, Margaret Rigby, for assault. It appeared that on Monday she took out a F ommons against him for being an habitual drunkard. On receipt of the summons he became very 25hu8ive, and early on Tuesday morning seized her by the throat and attempted to strangle her. The magistrates i•ent him to goal for three months, and the wife was granted a separation order with an allow- ance of 12s Gd weekly.

STREET BETTING. WARRINGTON MAN HEAVf LT FINED. GOOD THINGS" THAT DID NOT COME OFF. A street betting casein which a great deal of interest was manufested was heard at the flo,ongh Police Court on Monday when, before the Mayor and other magistrates, Walter Delooze, chimney sweep, 19. Wiuwick-road, waacharged with having been guilty of street netting in Old Gardens on Saturday. Mr. T. S. Steel defended and pleaded not guilty. Detective Holland said that in consequence of com- plaints having been made with reference to street betting in Old Gardens, he, along with Detective Woollacott, kept observation and on Saturday about 12.10 p.m. they saw the defendant take up tis stand in the Old Gardens. Between that time aid ne o'clock no fewer than ten persons went to the defendant arid handed over slips and money. The defendant put the money in his trousers pocket and also in the right band pocket of his jacket. After rash transaction with the men, the defendant went into a cottage. At one o'clock they arrested Delooze o said "Alright alright ; I will come with you. You have no nesd to frighten a man to death." On the way to the police station he said "It has just gone one. You have been rather quick. One o'clock is my time." On sesrching the defendant witness found a slip of paper eri which were the names of horses running at Haydock nak and Liogfield. In answer to the charge the defendant said " Did you see me take any ? I have not taken any bets." On searching him he also found 3s. Pd. in money, the silver in his trousers pocket and the copper in his jacket pocket. By Mr. Steel : We were fifty yards away keeping watch and there were some buildings between us, but our look-out was above them and we could see him quite plainly. Detective Woollacott gave corroborative evidence and, examined by the Chief Constable, he said he had known Delooze for years and could not have been mistaken in his identity. Inspector Hodgkiss, who was on duty in the charge office when the defendant was brought in, said he remarked to the prisoner that it was very foolish of him to get into such a position. The prisoner replied : "Yes. lam going to give it up ; it is a mug's game." He also admitted having been at the Old Gardens on the previous Thursday and Friday. Mr. Steel totally denied the charge, on the ground that an absolute mistake had been made in the identity of the prisoner. He thought that if the Bench saw the position of the building from which the observations were made, and the position of the entry in which it was alleged his client was standing, they would see that It was quite possible to have made a mistake in the MBO. lie himself had made a mistake, for he. went in the building and looked down, and he had mistaken another man for his client. .JThe Chief Constable: I object to these hilarious state- ments unless he is going to put them in as evidence and prove them. I shall cross-examine on them. Continuing, Mr. Steel maintained that a mistake had been made. The slip found in the defendant's posses- sion had been given to him by a young man who had recommended the horses as" good things." He would call evidence to prove that the defendant did not get home until 12.20 at noon. On oath Delooze said he came to town on Saturday morning and, after having collected some money for work he had done, he went round the market to Mill- street just before 12 o'clock. He called at a loan office in Mill-street to stand bondsman for a friend of his aad whilst there be met a young man who said be had got the names of four likely horses and if he (defend- ant) wanted them he could have them. They were then written down on a slip of paper and during the conversation the young man said he was going to Haydock Park races. He (defendant), left the loan office at a few minutes past 12 o'clock and he then went round the market again. He was not at Old Gardena at 12.10 and he had gone in the cottage to see Mrs. Steel about a picnic. lie did not do any betting. By the Chief Constable: What I said to Inspector Hodgkiss was " It is the first time and I hope it will be the last." I did not say the words he has given in his e sidence. A young man named Harold Harding, a clerk employed by the City Loan Co., Mill-street, said that on Saturday morning the defendant, along with another man, called at the °eke to do business. After the busi- ness had been conducted he entered into conversation with Delooze and said he was going to Haydock races in the afternoon. Delooze tsked him if he had anything good and he replied "Yes." He wrote the names of the horses down on the paper (produced) as Delonze had asked him to do so. The prisoner left their office about 12 o'clock. The Chief: Was it not nearer one ?—1 don't think £O. How do you remember the time ?—Witness appeared rather confused but in a minute or two said he was sure it was about 12 o'clock. The Chief : About?—Yes. None of the horses won ?—I don't know; I don't think so. The Chief: You seem to be as sure of the time as you were of the "good things." (Laughter). Did you give any other customer tips that morning? —No. The Chief : If you give tips like that you are likely to get many more clients coming to your place for loans. The Chief: How many customers had you that morning ?—About twenty. What time did the one previous to prisoner leave ? I could not say. The Chief : It looks singular you remembering the time this man left and not the others.-1 was not quite sure to the minute. After other witnesses had been called, the magis- trates retired and on their return Delooze was dried £5 and coats, (£5 16s. in all).
Borough Police Court.
MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen J Smethurst, James Evans and W Bolton, Councillor Wilkinson Messrs S Wright, W Furness, W Roberta and G Pang. . _ _

A LODGER'S THEFT.—Walter Edward Tomlin, a young man, of no fixed abode, was charged on remand with stealing on July 3rd from 16, Pierpoint-street, two watches, articles of jewellery and lOs in cash, valued in all at £2, the property of Edward Reardon.—The Chief Constable said that four weeks ago the prisoner came to Warrington and obtained lodgings at IS, Plerpoiet- street. He got work at Bewsey Forge and was earning 30s to 33s per week. He worked at the forge fcr a short time but absconded last week and the property was then missed.—The Chief Constable, after baying read previous convictions, said the man had an exceptionally bad record. He had come to Warrington penniless and starving and had done that mean trick to a fello lodger.—Prisoner was sent to caol for three months With bard labour.

THEFT OF JAM.—Benjamin Gaskell, of no fixed abode, was charged on remand with stealing on the 11th inst a pot of jam value 10d., the property of Mr William grocer, Buttermarket-street, Warrington.—At the previous hearing prisoner declared Ile boug4 the jam at Altrincham.—The Chief Constable said that it had since been ascertained that the jar of jam was similar to those in a large case which stood outside Mr Isaac's shop Three pots were missing. The straw found In the prisoner's pocket was the same as that in which the jars were enclosed.—Prisoner, who entirely denied the charge, said he had been " roughing it," and that accounted for the straw in his pocket.—The Chief Constable pointed out, and his statement was supported by witnesses' that the prisoner had stayed in Warring- ton the night previous to the theft. He was seen in the town at 6.20 on the morning of the 12th, so that he could not have bought the jam in Altrinobam or have walked from there that morning.—Gaskell was sent to prison for one month. A NEW SUMMER COSTUME.—Evidently overwhelmed by the excessive heat Patrick Moran, of no fixed abode, who was in custody on a charge of lodging out in Ship-yard during the week-end, divested himself of his garments in the cells on Sunday and tore them to shreds, thus leaving himself with little or no clothing in which to appear before the magistrates on Monday. However a slight covering had been made for him by the police and, as the Chief Constable pointed out, he made his appearance in the costume we have read about in Scripture—sack-cloth and ashes, minus the ashes.— Patrick, who smiled serenely, was sent to prison for two months. He had 49 previous convictions..

THREATENED TO TAKE HIS LlFE.—Ricbard Drury,of no fixed address, was charged with an offence tinder the Vagrancy Act.—The Chief Constable said that at 1-30 on Sunday morning P.C. Nicholls was in Winwick- street when he received a complaint to the effect that the prisoner was walking about with a bottle of poison which be had threatened to drink. It would appear that the prisoner had had a great deal of trouble but it was a question whether he had really intended to take the poison, Ile bad no visible means and he (the Chief), asked lota remand until Friday in the hope that some- thing could be arranged for him.—This course was agreed to, and on Friday the Chief said they did not think he had really intended to take his life and he asked that the prisoner might be given relief to enable him to go to Pendleton. The magistrates thought that was a proper course to adopt and dismissed the prisoner who was assisted on his way.

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.--Sfary Messitter, 38, Rose and I Crown-street, was charged with having attempted to commit suicide by strangling herself with a neck-tie.— The Chief Constable said the case was one in which the sympathy of the Court was due to the woman whose husband seemed to be responsible for the whole of the business, fie had been corning home beastly drunk for some time and had made use of the most filthy language towards his wife. On the Sunday night the husband went home and used vile language. The wife said she could stand it no longer and tried to strangle herself. I The neighbours, hearing screams, came to the house and the husband had a very rough passage for a moment or so. He (the Chief) thought it was a case which should be adjourned so that Mr Firth could bring his good offices to bear. The case was adjourned until Friday. The husband was then called into the box and asked what be was going to do. He said his wife was a very hysterical woman.—The Chairman : She looks a good woman. Are you prepared to take care of her in a manly manner ?—Yes, I have done so. If she thinks she will be happier with a separation order, for God's sake let her have it.—A magistrate : She would be all right if you were all right to her. The husband was known by one of the officers to be a most violent man —The Chairman : We have had an idea of what he was like 'this morning. On Friday when the case was heard again the charge was reduced to one of breach of the peace and the husband having promised to keep off the drink, and look after his wife, Mrs Messiter was placed under probation for 12 months.

TUESDAY.—Before Councillor Jackson Holmes (in the chair), Dr Fox and Lieutenant-Colonel Edelsten. ALLISGED Iltcvcut THErr.—Robert Clayton, of no fixed abode, was charged with stealing a bicycle on Saturday, the property of Harry Thomas, of Stockport. Chief Inspector Williamson, in asking for a remand for a week, said that on Saturday afternoon, at about 5.30, the prosecutor went into a restaurant in Market-street. He left his bycycle in the front shop while he had some refreshments in another room. Prisoner entered the shop, tooktthe bicycle and rode away. No trace could be found of the cycle until the prisoner offered it for sale in Liverpool on Saturday. The prisoner was apprehended by a Liverpool detective. When charged with the offence he replied : " Yes." Clayton was remanded for a week.

THURSDAY.—Before Mr J Rymer Young (in the chair) Messrs A J Jolley, W Roberts, W I: Williams, J Upson, Dr Fox and Dr Naden. A WomaN's FOLLY.—Annie Williams, 2, Mottrarns- yard, was charged with stealing from the house in which she resides, a chair value 33 6d, the property of her husband. She was also summoned for being an habitual drunkard. The Chief Constable said that the prisoner left home the previous Thursday, and on Tuesday while her husband was asleep, she went in the house, took the chair and pawned it. After evidence had been given of the woman's drinking habits, the magistrates granted a separation order with an allowance of 3s Gd per week Proceedings were not taken in the first case. WINDOW BREAKERS.—A number of youths were each fined ss. for breaking windows on the premises of Messrs Bowman, Ltd., Lythgoes-lane on the Ist July. Damage of an extensive nature was done and Mr Amos who appeared for the company said the firm had suffered continually through windows being broken.—A number of lads were fined ss. each for breaking windows in the Latchford Tannery on the 7th July.

FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Pierpoint, Messrs G Pilling, A J Jolley, S Wright, W Furness and Dr Fox. BET OS A SUMMONS,—WiIIiam Willis, Thelwall-lane, was charged with having been in a passage in Thelwall- lane the previous day for the purpose of street betting.

div.head: BOY SCOUTS AT OLD ENGLISH FAIR.
div.p: BOY SCOUTS AT OLD ENGLISH FAIR.
CAMP AND CHURCH PARADE.

During last week-end various troops were in camp at the Old English Fair, Victoria Park. The Ist W arrington troop were in camp on the Wednesday, the other troops not arriving until Saturday. During Wednesday, Thursday and Friday i nights the scouts n camp gave gieat assistance in guarding the property in the various marquees. Mr. J. B. Starkey was in charge of the camp and he was ably assisted by Scoutmaster Bennett. On Thursday, Friday and Saturday the scouts made themselves useful in quite a number of ways by selling pro- grammes, aerial post cards, guessing tickets and other articles. Their services were several times requisi- tioned for the purpose of finding children who were lost. On Friday and Saturday a cycle stores was opened, one of the scouts' small marquees serving as
MR. J. B. STARKEY `AND THE TROOPS.
a store. This proved beneficial to the cyclists attending the fair....

On Saturday the following troops entered camp and stayed until Sunday night :-Ist Orford (Scoutmaster Shepherd), Ist Winwick (Scoutmaster Owen), Ist Widnes, Farnworth (Scoutmasters Early and A S M Dunstan), 2nd Widnes (Hon Scoutmaster Lloyd; Scoutmaster Roberts and Assistant Scoutmaster Sweetman) and let Earlestown (Scoutmaster Huxley). Assistant Scoutmasters Anderson (sth Widnes) and Abrams (Ist Weston Point), together with several of their scouts visited the camp during the week-end. The arrival of the different troops created a great deal of interest among the crowds of people in the fair, and the erection of tents and cooking of meals proved quite an eye-opener to some.
Photo, Burn

On Sunday previous to breakfast Scoutmaster Huxley conducted a short service, the boys being formed around the Union Jack. At 9.30 the scouts assembled for church parade and headed by the bugle band they proceeded to the Parish Church. Hon. Scoutmaster Walsh was in charge, and Messrs. J. B. Starkey and R. Lees accompanied. The various troops made preparations for departure soon after tea. Before departing the troops paraded before the flag and saluted. The Farnworth and Widnes and Earles- town troops left just before seven o'clock for their march home, where they safely arrived about nine o'clock. The Ist Warrington troop were the last to leave, they having to see to the clearing up of the camping ground. Three cheers were given for Mr. Starkey and others who had made the camp a success.

Prisoner pleaded guilty. Detective Wool!scot proved the case and said that from 11.30 to one o'clock he saw several working men go to the prisoner and hand him betting slips and money. When arrested Willis replied "It's alright I had the papers on me, I was going to chuck it up this week." There were 25 slips and £2 Ta Gd found on the prisoner when he was searched. The Chief Constable said that amongst the bets was one on the back of a summons, signed by one of the magistrates. The Mayor : Contempt of court I should think. (Laughter.) One of the bets enumerated on the slip was "6d. to win on Policeman." A Magis- trate: Was there nothing on the magistrate? (Laughter.) Willis was fined £2 18s. SOLD COAL TO GET DRINK.—Mary Foy, was summoned by her husband, Thomas, for being at habitual drunkard.—Fov stated that he was a tanner's labourer and that his wife was never in the house but always out drinking. He also accused her of getting bread from the shoo and selling it for drink. She had also sold buckets of coal for the sake of" penny gills." —A separation order was granted Foy having to pay his wife 2s Gd per week. AN ADJOURNMENT.—Thomas Hewitt was summoned by his wife Mary for being an habitual drunkard.—Mr T S Steel appeared for the complainant and Mr W H J Jenkins defended.—After hearing the opening statement of Mr Steel,corroborated by the complainint the magis- trates thought that it would be to the interests of both parties if the case was adjourned for three months and this was accordingly done.

trch of England's Men's Society. The progress of the Church of England Men's Society in this district is evidenced by the formation of a branch in connection with the Warrington Parish Church. A large number of members were initiated by the Rev G C Briggs, vicar:of Christ Church, Latchford, at a special initiation service held on Sunday afternoon. The first portion was the ordinary service set out for the C.E.M.S., which was conducted by the Rector and the Rev G C Briggs, and this was followed by the initiation service. An address was given by the Rev G C Briggs to a large congregation, which included members of other branches of the society in the district.
