div.head: Social Volcano.
div.p: Social Volcano.

Bishop's Appeal to Leisured People. The Bishop of Liverpool, preaching at St. Peter's Church, Formby, on Tuesday night, appealed to the leisured classes to show more practical sympathy towards the poor. He said he need not remind them thal they were living on the edge of a volcano. The balance of power had shifted itself on to the shoulders of the working classes. The strikes last August, and at the beginning of the year, were foretastes of what was to come unless there was more sympathy shown between class and class. There were thousands of people in the towns little better than the Pagans, people who, on the slightest provocation would, if they thought they could gain anything, at once go out on strike. The Bishop lamented also the dying out of Sunday observance. It was becoming a day of pleasure, he said, while motoring, golfing, and tennis playing were taking the place of worship. If the custom of observing Sunday as a day of rest died out, it was ominous for the future of the English people.

div.head: Disestablishers at Chester Diocesan Conference. . _
div.p: Disestablishers at Chester Diocesan Conference. . _

At the Chester Diocesan Conference on Wednesday, the Archdeacon of St. Asaph delivered an address on the Welsh Church Bill, and moved :—" That, in the opinion of this conference, the Government bill for disestablishing and disendowing the four Welsh dioceses thereby dismembering the Church of England, is based upon wholly insufficient grounds ; is unwise and inequitable in its proposals; and affords no promise of good at all commensurate with the damage it will inflict upon Christian feeling and Christian work." The Archdeacon of Chester seconded the resolution. While the Bishop was putting the resolution, a lay delegate said :—I protest. I think the conduct of this meeting is just one of those things that lays the Church open to charges. I think it would have been fairer to have allowed the minority, who very likely are present, my lord, to have expressed their protest. You have arranged for two speakers to speak in defence of this Church, and not one to put the side of the minority, of whom I am one, which is, I think, hardly fair, my lord. The Bishop : May I say I gave the opportunity for your expression. (Loud applause). The Delegate : lam afraid I failed to catch your last words.
The Bishop : I really gave the opportunity for expression of the view which you are now, at a some- what late stage, expressing, before I made up my mind to put the resolution.

The Delegate: Pardon me, it was my idea to wait till you sat down, and give me the opportunity of speaking. (Cries of" Sit down ! The Bishop : Let us be perfectly fair to this gentle- man. I think the best thing we can do is to give this gentleman five minutes. (Applause.) The Delegate said that among the minority there were many who loved the Church as well as the majority did. He was a keen supporter of the Church, for which he had been a worker all his life. Yet he did not bold the views of the gentleman who moved the resolution. There was a large and growing number in the Estab- lished Church who were in full agreement with the disestablishment of the Welsh Church. (Cries of " No, no.") He said a large and growing number. He did not for a moment claim there was anything like a majority, only that their numbers were growing, and while they held that view they also held the Welsh Church in the highest esteem.

The resolution was carried with two dissentients. The conference passed a resolution expressing the opinion that it was desirable to adopt, as far as possi- ble, the methods of applying the recommendations con- tained in the report of the Archbishop's Committee on Church Finance to the diocese. Mr. Christie Miller said if the county could maintain a pack of foxhounds at an annual expenditure of £lO,OOO, it could afford more than £3,000 for the diocesan institutions.

The Bishop of Chester said the amount raised for Church purposes in the diocese was about £170,G00 a year. Mr. Lunt of Elworth.—Supposing your lordship said, "I am prepared to give afifth or a tenth of my in- come," and all the clergy did likewise, would it not be an inspiration to the parishioners. (Laughter)? The Bishop raid it was an excellent proposition, but he was not sure that he was prepared to make the offer. Baptist Church, Latchford. The congregation of the Baptist Church Latchford were gratified to have another visit from the Rev. J. F. Matthews, of Sheffield, a former pastor of the church who preached at the anniversary sermons on Sunday. Each service was largely attended and Mr. Matthews' thoughtful and convincing discourses were listened to with great interest and appreciation. The service held in the afternoon was largely of a musical character, anthems, solos, and quartettes being admirably rendered i by the choir. Special music was also ntroduced at the other services, and the singing throughout reflected cridit not only upon the members of the choir, but upon the organist, Mr. Peter Harrison. The preacher took

fcr his text in the evening the words : "For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord " (Luke ii. 7). The collectiou, which were in aid of the church funds, amounted to .Eli is 6d.

Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. There was a good meeting on Sunday presided over by Mr. Himsworth.The Rev. W Cooper gave the address upon the early efforts of Payton, the great Missionary ; his whole dependetce upon God, for guidance, preserva- tion and success, and God did deliver him. He experienced the Divine Succour, in his early bereave- ment by the loss of his wife, and he realized the manifold goodness of God. Mr Moon sang " Nazaieth" and the "Bell-ringer," which were much enjoyed, Mr. McEachren read the lesson. 'The president, led the prayer. _ _ _

St. John's Presbyterian Church. Taking as his subject on Sunday evening the " Benedictus" Rev. W. Reid referred to its constitution in several strophes. There appeared the song of one in darkness, borrowing from the literature of his land the anxious words and trembling notes expressive of pain. The childless home was a shadow and psin which never depsrted from his heart. But there appeared also the song of one who in darkness was stayed by the Divine promises, recognised not only in the word of God but in His every action. The movement of pro- mise into prayer constituted the next step in which every life which was able to grasp his relationship with environment, and intelligently read God in every- thing, made supplication, even if mute, truly seen in trustful acquiescence. The song then was seen to be that of one who saw the dawn, or the day in anticipa- tion. Every lie is anticipated and we to-day shape very largely the lives of the next generation. The day- spring is seen reddening into perfection. Pure rays stream their light into deep valleys of darkness, and the Canticle which opened amid the gloom has led the imprisoned soul into the perfect day.

div.head: Visit of the Rev. J. D. Jones.
div.p: The Visit of the Rev. J. D. Jones.

Wycliffe Congregational Church, Bewsey-street, was favoured on Sunday by the presence of the Rev. J. D. Jones, M.A., B.D , of Bournemouth, ex-chairman of the Congregational Union. The visit of this distinguished preacher drew large congregations, many members of other churches in the town taking advantage of the opportunity of hearing him. They were delighted by his quiet, argumentative and well reasoned discourses and charmed by his mellifluous voice and pleasing countenance. The service of praise was heartily joined in by the choir and congregation. Two anthems were sung by the choir under the conductorship of Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac., that in the evening being enhanced by the artistic solo singing of Mr. W. Booth in Foster's setting "Oh, for a closer walk with God." At the morning service Mr Jones delivered a brief address to the children, illuminated by short stories, on the theme "Don't care." He gave several instances showing how young people bad been able to face death with indifference when fortified by the conviction that they were acting riehtly. He advised his young bearers to let the fear of God dominate their lives and then like Sir Henry Lawrence it might be said of them : He feared no man because he feared God so much." The sermon for older folk was based on the twin texts " Honour have all His saints " (Psalm 149 v. 9) and "They glorified God in Me" (Galatians, chapter 1 24th verse). These texts, he said, show what God is to man, and what man ought to be, and sometimes is to God. Man and God were inter•dependent. Man depended upon God, and strange as it might seem, God depended upon man. Through man, God carried his purposes into effect. In developing this theme, the preacher showed bow men became really great when they glorified God. In the long run the verdict of the world was true. He contrasted the contemporary lives of Nero, the then emperor of the world end the despised St. Paul,and said history bad now adjusted their relative positions. Draw- ing a distinction between honours and honour, the preacher demonstrated how the world could confer the former' hut only goodness of character could command honour. Turning to the second text, the preacher observed that men could and did bring honour and glory to God by their lives, and gave several instances. Many a man bad been led to :revere and worship God by a saintly life. The majority of people to-day were outside the churches and chapels. Ele wondered sometimes whether the pre- vailing indifference to religion could not be placed at the door of professedly Christian people. What was wanted was not better preaching in the churches but better living. Men judged Christianity by what they saw of Christ's followers, and it behoved all Christians to live lives that would bring honour and glory to God.

The evening discourse was based on the text" Jesus seeing their faith saith unto the sick of the palsy, son be of good cheer," (Matthew ix, 2). Referring to the optimism of Robert Browning's "Swan song," the preacher said there was really only one person who had lived up to the high standard of Browning's ideal and that was Jesus Christ. The secret of Christ's indomitable hopefulness in all the dark days of His life was to be found in his faith in the Father- hood of God. The rreacher deprecated any doubt as to the ultimate triumph of the gospel of Christ and said the key-note of Christ's message was courage. Collections were taken on behalf of Lancashire Independent College and Sileoates School. The Mothers' Union.

A meeting of the Mother,' Union in the Rural Deanery of Winwick was held in the Co-operative 'fall, Cairo-street, on Wednesday afternoon. About 400 members came from the parishes of Warrington, Newton, Earlestown, Ashton, Uolborne, Burtonwood and Haydock. The chair was taken by the Rural Dean (Canon Willis) who was supported on the platform by the Rev T R Matthews, vicar of Earlestovrn, Rev A M Mitchell, of Burtonwood, Mrs Rylands, Mrs Willis and other ladies. The proceedings opened • with prayer and hymn, after which the Chairman wel- comed the members and expressed his gratifica- tion at seeing so many present. Ile then called upon Mrs Steinthal, diocesan secretary for the Ripon Mothers' Union, to give an address. She gave the members excellent advice on how to keep their homes happy and peaceful, by contented minds,superior to environment, founded on real faith in God. The address was illustrated ,with many telling anecdotes. A vote of thanks to the Speaker and chairman proposed by the Rev T R Matthews, seconded by Rev A AI Mitchell and supported by Mrs [glands, was carried with acclamation. At the conclusion of the meeting, tea WBS handed round, after which all adjourned to the Rectory garden,where a verypleasent evening was spent.

NEW ATLANTIC PORT.—By the annexation of the territory of Ungava the Province of Quebec has obtained a splendid winter port which is destined, says Mgr. Blanche, Vicar Apostolic of the district, to become one of the most important on the Atlantic. This harbour is at Sept Iles, and is open all the year round, and is large enough to contain the whole British Fleet. It is closer to Europe than any other of the Atlantic seaports, and is an expellent port of refuge, being protected by the mountains from severe storms.

The dilatoriness of the Local Government Board in sanctioning plans for the provision of douche baths at the Bolton Council school called forth criticisms at the meeting of the Warrington Education Committee held at the Town Hall on Monday evening. Councillor H Roberts presided and there were also present ;—Mr A J Jolley (deduty-chairman), Alderman A Bennett, Coun- cillors T Birtles, W H J Jenkins, J T Locker, C Jackson Holmes, J Pemberton, W H Bellian, R Hen- shall. J Wilkinson, T S Steel, Rev Father N Wilson, Mrs C Jackson Holmes; Messrs C E Parker, E Plinston, J Upson, C 11 Unsworth, G Walker, R T Fairclough and J Moore Murray (director). RESIGNATION OF THE REV. JAMES DAVIES The DIRECTOR read a letter from the Rev. James Davies, intimating that be had forwarded to the Rev. Canon Willis, president of the Warrington Association of Foundation Managers of Church of England Schools, his resignation as one of their representatives on the Education Committee. He tendered his sincere acknow- ledgement of the unfailing courtesy extended to him [during his membership of the authority. The CHAIRMAN I think I shall only be expressing the general opinion of the members of the committee when I say we receive that resignation with consider- able regret. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Davies has been a very useful member of our committee and a gentleman for whom we all entertain feelings of respect and regard. I don't know what the cause of his resignation is, but, whatever it is, I regret it. THE INSURANCE QUESTION. When the minutes of the Finance Committee were submitted Mr. FAIRCLOUGH asked the Chairman (Mr. Jolley) what the cost of insurance of caretakers and other servants of the authority would be? Mr. Jolley: I cannot tell you that. We have pro- vided for a deduction in the accounts passed for pay- ment. _

The CHAIRMAN: Probably at the next meeting Mr. Jolley will be able to tell you, it is not a question to be answered easily. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH: I thought he might know. Councillor PEMBERTON : If it is in these accounts, ought he not to be prepared to answer now? At the next meeting it may not be in order if we asked about anything that is not on the agenda. That is the unfor- tunate part of these meetings. Mr. JOLLEY: Unfortunately I am not infallible like Councillor Pemberton—(laughter I—and therefore I must plead ignorance—quite honestly. lam very sorry I don't know as much as he does. Counnillor PEMBERTON : I don't say I am infallible. (Laughter.) I thought Mr. Jolley was snch a good Chancellor of the Exchequer that he would know what he had put in to meet, the insurance charges. The CHAIRMAN: I think we have Mr. Jolley's assur- ance that he will give the information to the committee at the first opportunity. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH : lam staisfied with that. SCHOOL EXEMPTIONS.

- "THE SOFTER PART OF THE COMMITTEE." A discuseion having been raised at a meeting of the School Attendance Committee (after due notice by a member of the Committee) upon the question of the exemption from school attendance by the committee, it was, in the end, resolved, that, in future. applications for exemption from attendance at school shall only be dealt with at a special meeting of the School Attend- ance Committee to be held for the purpose once each month ; and that all previous resolutions dealing with this subject be amended accordingly. Consideration of the question of exemption being granted on an educational qualification only was adjourned to the next meeting of the committee. Mr. PussroN, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said they involved a new departure which was being adopted with a view to getting out of a difficulty which unfortunately had existed for some time. Some months ago the Committee endeavoured to alter the regulations RS to the system of dealing with school exemptions by introducing a reso ution referring to the " neoessitous " and " beneficial "parts of exemptions. That had been in force up to the present time hut the method by which the Committee had dealt with the cases was such that an alteration was felt to he necessary. At present there was a rota of members for each meeting. On the Committee were men with different opinions with reference to the school age,the necessity for children to contribute to the family earn- ings, and as to what constituted beneficial employment. Some members believed that the only way of settling the question was to make children attend the school until they were fourteen years of age. (Hear, hear.) Others believed that if a child had reached the age of thirteen and had made satisfactory attendances he ought to be exemptei from school under almost circumstances. There was this unfortunate position : When the more tender part of the Committee were present—

The -CHAIRMAM : Do you mean the 'softer part ? (Lstighter). Mr PLINSTON : I think I will leave it for other members to sty that. Councillor HENSHALL : He means the more reasonable. Mr PLINSTON said that when the more tender portion of the committee were present, they would grant exemptions which another section of the committee would not think of allowing. That there should be such a difference of method on different days was not fair to the committee, the parents or the children. The object of the new resolution Was to call upon the whole of the committee once a month to deal with exemptions. Councillor BELLIAN seconded and the minutes were passed. CIRCUMLOCUTION OFFICE. PROTEST AGAINST LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD DELAY. It was noted by the Sites and Buildings Committee ' that the contractor for the extension of the Bolton Council school had withdrawn his tender of November last for the erection of the douche baths, owing to the excessive advance in the prices of materials in the meantime. It was decided to request the law Clerk to inform the Local Government Board of this effect of their delay in sanctioning the loan for this purpose, and to ask them to furnish the committee with any explanation there may be of such delay. Mr. FAIRCLOUnir, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the committee applied to the Local Government Board for a loan over five months ago but could not get any reply. Such a long delay placed the committee in a very awkward position and it was only right and proper that they should ask for an explanation. Mr. WALKER seconded. Alderman BENNETT said he was glad the committee bad taken that course. The Town Council had been so much criticised by the Local Government Board for certain little idiosyncracies of theirs that one felt rather glad to be able to pay them back in their own coin and to point .out that municipalities were not the only people who did not always do their duty promptly. He sincerely hoped that the delay did not mean that there was to be any change of policy in the attitude of the Board towards the baths questicn. Personally he regarded the introduction of douche bathe in the schools as one of the most hopeful progressive signs that had ever come before the Committee. Those who bad 3tudied the question would realize that douche

baths in all the new schools would be an enormous: advantage and would tend to the health and cleanline _ of the children. facturers would find it profitable to produce it. It is obvious then that the tendency of values is to become proportionate to labour required. This law of course deals only with commodities produced and consumed on a normal scale. Things like rare pictures and books cannot be considered in this way. Let us take another case. Hero are a number of miners digging for gold. There is a demand for water, so one of them leaves his work and walking to a spring some miles away brings back two pails of water. Now on what basis will he exchange this water for gold? Obviously he will want as much gold as he could have got had he remained digging. If he asked more than this the miners would go themselves or some would bring water for less than his price. Let us now imagine that a company takes over the gold digging and another the supply of water for the mining camp. We see that the com- modities must still exchange on a labour time basis. If the water company gives water, which it takes say ten men to pro- duce, for gold which is produced by eight men, it is obvious that the company will not, other things being equal, pay as good dividends as the gold mining company. To remedy this they will put up the price of water and as the gold mining company cannot do it better for itself or get any other company to do it, they will pay. If now we bring in many other companies producing all the ordinary necessaries of life, the case is not changed fundamentally. In those industries which return a good profit there will be plenty of production and competition. Capital always seeking the best profits tends by overworking the profitable industries and leaving the unprofitable, to make for a uniform profit. This flow of capital has the result that commodities tend to exchange on the basis of the labour time required to pro- duce them. Comparing different industries we see that approximately the divisions of labour into brain, skilled and unskilled, are the same. We may now state the general law of value. The value of a commodity is deter- mined by the necessary labour time required to produce it. The law does not refer to any particular article but to a commodity as a class produced and exchanged under normal conditions.

To sum up. A commodity is useful and must have been made from nature by labour. The average commercial exchange ratio between two commodities is expressed by their value. Price is the temporary exchange ratio between any commodity and gold, the standard commodity. Value is not deter- mined by supply and demand nor by utility, but by the necessary labour time required to produce the commodity. In a future article it will be seen that labour time is itself a commodity, its value being determined in the same way as other commodities. W. BAGULEY.

div.head: SHIP CANAL RAILWAY SCHEME.
div.p: SHIP CANAL RAILWAY SCHEME.

The Manchester Ship Canal Company are about to commence an important undertaking. A tunnel is to be built at the Barton Aqueduct with the object of connecting the company's railway lines on the right bank of the canal. These lines at present terminate on either side of the aqueduct, and through traffic from some works to the dock railway system, which connects with the six great trunk lines of the country, has not, in consequence been possible. But when the tunnel Is completed and the lines are connected the facilities for direct communication will be perfected and will doubtless be largely used.

CANADIAN BANK STATEMENT.—The May statement ' of the Canadian Banks is interesting from the fact that the total public deposits for the first time exceed the billion dollar mark (200 millions sterling). Of that sum 377 millions is money at call and 625 millions deposits subject to notice, the letter being generally understood to represent the savings of the people.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
THE SUPERANNUATION QUESTION AGAIN

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, Mr. E. L. 13 'rat presiding. There were also present : Mrs Simpson, Rev A M Mitchell, Messrs A J Jolley (vice-chairman), J Billinge. A Brooks, W Houghton, W C Brooks, W Furness, R Lee, J A Rushwolth, J A Hughes, W Flnnsgan, G Allen, M W Seton, T Ritchie, Evans, A Bottomley (clerk) It I Partridge (assistant clerk), and W J Brown (master). div.head: NEW WATER TANK.
div.p: NEW WATER TANK.
The Building CO-Mmittee, after consultation with Mr Segar Owen, recommended that a water tank with a capacity of 15,000 gallons be erected.
- E TEM PE RANCE LECTURE.

The CLERK read a letter from Mr Benjamin T Parkes, secretary of the Warrington Citizens' Temperance League, stating that at a meeting of the Executive Corn mittee a resolution was passed expressing thanks to the Guardians for having granted permission for a lecturer of the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Elope Union to give a scientific temperance lecture to the children at the Padgate Cottage Homes. We trust" concluded the reselution" That the lectures will be productive of much good and that the children will receive therefrom lessons which will help them to become worthy citizens of our country."

div.head: CANCER RESEARCH.
div.p: CANCER RESEARCH.

At the annual meeting of the Imperial Cancer Research Fund, on Wednesday, Sir John M'Fadyean said that the knowledge of tumour formation was much more precise than it was ten years ago. It had still, unfortunately, to be admitted that numbers of points remained in obscurity. The ultimate goal of investiga- tion must be the discovery of the cause and prevention of cancer, and it was certain that could be reached only by researches such as that pursued in the laboratories of the fund.

div.head: ANGLING TIT-BITS.
div.p: ANGLING TIT-BITS.

"Romancing," did I bear someone whisper? Nay, I leave that sort of thing to the professionals. And, among the, where shall we find the "champion." It is written that until the rise of the golf liar the angling liar held pride of place in the gallery of imaginative conversationalists. but I don't know about that. I am a diligent r,.ader of the local angling notes, and I have often been struck by the extreme modesty and reticence of the contributor of the brief weekly record. When, as not infrequently happens, members of the local association have but indifferent suceess, " A.S." just tells the brutal truth, and there the matter ends. Well, what's to be done about it? Somebody's reputation is at stake. Whenever I have ventured on a word of remonstrance in the interests of the gentle craft, writes the inimitable ac;nteur in question —there have been known cases in which the precise accuracy of the angler has been challenged. There is, for instance, the yam of the men who were having a crack in the smoke-room corner, when one of them recalled an mcident in connection with his grandfather, who, he said, had stood eight feet six inches in his stockinged feet. I have found it useful to appeal to Mr. Carter Platte for the needful to kind o' balance things. May I supplement, after that fashion now, and so try to make up for the element which one misses from the plain, matter of fact story of the weekly doings of our local anglers? "Here, draw it mild. Say six feet six inches," suggested one of his hearers, an angler. "Sir," retorted the narrator indignantly, "I am drawing it mild. As a matter of absolute fact my grandfather stood eight feet six and a half inches in his stockinged feet." After that none cared to dispute the matter further, but the angler, in sheer self-defence, com- menced a yarn about his catching a trout in the Wharfe which weighed thirty-seven pounds, and measured fifty-six inches in length. At once his hearers chorused their doubts. "Fact," said the angler, unabashed. "But it's impossible—simply, absurdly impossible. You'll really have to make your trout a bit less than that before we can believe it," they cried. "Very well, then," chirped the angler cheerfully,"you get him to take half a yard off his grand- father, and then I'll see what I can do with my trout." Again one celebrated Yorkshire fisherman's dog was even warranted, when his master's dies got caught up in a tree on the opposite side of the river, to swim across, climb the tree, and release the cast. Another was in the habit of accompanying his owner when fishing a club length of stream where the limit size for tak able fish was nine inches. The dog, as was his custom before the'size limit was introduced, jumped in and brought out in his mouth fish after fish as s as they were hooked, but after a while seemed to got sort of discouraged when his master carefully measured all the fish and threw half of them into the water again. The dog watched the angler's strict attention to the new regulation for a time, and then retired up the bank, and leaned against a tree to think. The consequence was that as soon as that dog reached home he hunted round for a measure, bit a notch in his tail exactly nine inches from the end, and the next time he went fishing measured all the fish he landed against his tail, and pitched back all those under the limit size.

THE ULTIMATE AUTHORITY. In this paper last week was mentioned the case of a witness at an inquest who declined to take an oath because the Bible says "Swear not at all." I have come across people who were capable of interpreting the injunction as admitting of their swearing if not "at all," at least at some. The other day I had a little discussion with a Christadelpidan, and some remark of his led me to rder to the case of the peni- tent thief on the cross, and Christ's assurance as to his immediate blissful destiny. " Ah, but," objected my flien, "you don't punctuate the passage properly; put the comma in the right places and it makes a world of difference.'Verily, vetily, I say unto thee this day, thou shalt he with ine in Paradise." You read it as if it was a promise that be should be with Him in Paradise that very day ; but the ' this day ' is to be understood as simply the equivalent of now.'

I"You shall be with Me,' said Jesus ; I say so now this day and say it." " Oh," said I, "if it comes to taking such liberties with Scripture, ono might read "Peter stood at the wicket and cried out" as a cricket item ; and " Peter lodged with one Simon a tanner " as a banking transaction. LoJking the reproach for which be was unable to find adequate expression at the moment, my Christadelphian friend passed sorrowfully on his way. ' PUZZLING BOUNDARIES.

The question raised respecting Warrington ind the Cheshire boundary recalled certain experiences of my own at Todmorden, where Mr. B. S. *Townroe is just now busy. When I used to go there as a reporter, it was common for speakers from the Town Hall plat- form to indulge in facetious speculations as to their precise whereabouts. " You Lancashire people," one would begin—and then suddenly halt and ask if he cught to say "Yorkshire people," adding: "The fact is, I do not know whether I am standing in Lancashire or in Yorkshire." It all depended on tha exact ' position occupied at the moment, the stream dividing the two counties running beneath the hall. Todmor- den is in three Parliamentary divisions—Middleton, Sowcrby, and Clitheroo. The assistant overseer must enjoy the preparation of the lists of voters, and the political agents have a _high old time at the annual revision.

HAROLD. " Where was Harold ? " So ran a conundrum sub- mitted by the Editor of this paper a week ago, the reference being to Mr. Harold Smith, MP. It some- how brought to my mind a good old " wheeze " which a certain schoolmaster tried to palm off on my innocent self perhaps a couple of years or so ago —in fact, when last the Easter conference of the National Teachers' Union was held down Hasiings way. The same ancient story has been told of the old "Victory" and Nelson, and if I repeat it as adapted to the Battle of Hastings and the death of King Harold, I must do it in my own way. Here, in a nutshell, is my version of the incident :
A Hastings guide with tourists close at heel Led past the spot where noble Harold fell. "Aye," snapped a Yorkshire dame "an' he mud wee!;

.Kw varry nearly tummled theer mysel ! " BOTANICAL SZECIMENS. The discovery of a rare orchid was announced in last Saturday's " Examiner." Some other choice specimens exist here and there, but the secret is jealously guarded by botanists ; once out, the rare plants would as certainly disappear from the face of the earth as a rare bird is bound to do as soon as the cheerful idict with a gun gets within range of it.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
DANGEROUS.

The picture of Howley Bridge, looking along the footway, reminded me of the trestle bridge which some readers may have seen above Hardcastle Crags in Yorkshire. The latest additions to the Halifax Corporation waterwcrks, in the shape of three large reservoirs, are on the moors some miles beyond, and as the navvies engaged thereupon were lodged in huts overlooking the Crags, they were conveyed to and from work hy means of a railway specially constructed for the conveyance of materials As there was a gorge to be crossed, this necessitated the temporary erection of a trestle bridge at a height of perhaps CO yards or so. Once my wife and I ventured to croas this on foot, and as there was gaps all tho way along it was a memorable experience. Moreover, when NY 3 were about midway, we heard the train rumbling along in the distance, and we had to hurry. True, there was a recess for the convenience of men working on the bridge, but it seemed in a rotten state as if it had not been used for some time. As a matter of fact, not long after our visit a woman sought refuge in it, and the woodwork gave way beneath her weight, with the result that she was precipitated to the depths and lost her life. NO. 1. I note that Alderman Bennett was determined to be the first passenger over the bridge above referred to, and that he incurred personal risk as well as making pecuniary sacrifice to ensure this. I can understand the feeling. In a sense it is that of the man who pays fancy prices f r first editions, I recall anothsr little experience of my own. Many years -ago a Free Library was opened in the town in which I then resided. The ceremony was pet formed by the Mayor, and his Worship took out the first book. I made haste to secure the next ticket, but presently lost it, and I have never been able to recover it. Thus the evidence of my cherished if modest distinction is destroyed, whereas Alderman Bennett can never ho robbed of his ; to the end of his eays he will be in a position proudly to boast of his achievement, and doubtless the memory of the great event will be kept green by his successon. One of these days (who shall say other- wise ?) it may be permanently recorded by means of a tablet.

div.head: FATAL HESITATION.
div.p: FATAL HESITATION.
---- Motor Fatality at Grappenhall.
DRIVER EXONERATED FROM BLAME.

A motor car fatality occurred in Knutsford-road, Grappenhall, on Saturday evening, the victim being John George Gleave, age 78 years, of Mayfield-road, Grappenhall. The circumstances were inquired into by Mr H C Yates, coroner, in the Parish Room, Grappen- hall, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr I? R Roberts appeared for the relatives and Mr A Browne for the driver of the c tr. _ .

Mary Gleave, wife of the deceased, said her husband went for a walk at 530 on Saturday evening. He was then quite well. At 6.30 he was brought home bleeding from a deep wound on the top of the head. Dr. Jago attended him but he died at midnight. The sight of deceased's left eye was deficient and he wai very deaf. The Coroner : You told the police he was blind in one eye. Da you wish to alter that ? itneEs : One eye was defective. The foreman of the jury (Mr. Billinge) : I believe he could not distinguish people. The Coroner: Do you think it wise to let him go for walks alone, in these days of motor cars ? Witness : Ha would have been insulted if we had not. He objected to anyone going with him. Harry Alfred Thompson, of Legh Villas, Knutsford- road, said he had a conversation with the deceased in Knutsford-road at 620 on Saturday evening. Deceased left him, saying he was going home. lie attempted to cross the road but when about half-way across, he hesitated momentarily. The Coroner : Was a horn blown ? Witness : I must confess I did not hear a motor horn or see the car until it was close up• Witness, continuing, said that just as deceased hesitated, a motor car appeared. Deceased was caught by it and fell in the roadway, the car striking his head. The Coroner: I think you say the car was being driven at a slow speed ?—I do, most emphatically. Witness stated that he was so confused that he could not say whether the driver did everything possible to avoid the accident.

Alexander Jack, of Kintsford-road, said that when in the middle of the road, the deceased appeared to lose his balance and not to know what to do. Ile turned back but afterwards went forward again and that was the cause of the accident. The driver of the car appeared to see the deceased in the road and slowed down to the lowest possible minimum, lie did every- thing he could to avoid the accident, crossing to his wrong side in order to miss the deceased. Witness did not think the car actually knocked the deceased down. He was so confused that he fell upon the oar, was twisted round and finally fell on his back in the road- way. His head must have struck some portion of the car. The Coroner : I gather from your evidence that the hesitation cost him his life. If he had gone straight across he would have been safe ? Witnoss : Yes. Did the driver sound his horn before the accident ? Yes' but I don't think the deceased saw the car or heard the horn in time. In answer to Mr. Roberts, witness said the oar would probably not be going above five miles an hour when he first saw it. The driver slowed down almost to a standstill. .

Mr Browne : Then the whole of the responsibility rested upon the deoeased ? Witness: I could not say. It seemed to be one of those things that had to be. It was purely an accident. Louis Cedric Baldur Smith,24 years of age,mechanical engineer' 40, Desmond-street, Liverpool, stated that on Saturday he was engaged by Mr. George Whittaker to drive a 38 horse power Daimler oar from Liverpool to Buxton and back. His instructions were to drive slowly, as the passengers were somewhat nervous. When nearing (lrappenhall on the return journey,he was travel' big at 18 miles an hour when he saw two men talking in ithe middle of the road.He sounded his horn and slowed down, applying both the hand and foot brakes. One or two people on the side of the road seemed to beckon and shout to the men who seemed to notice the car and made for the side of the road on which it was travelling. To avoid them, witness turned to his wrong side. Deceased then hesitated for a moment turned round and hurried back to the side he had started from, just as the car was on a level with him. Witness saw deceased pass him on the left but, hearing a shout, he pulled up and found deceased lying in the roadway. Deceased appeared to have come into contact with the hinges of the door of the car, as there were pieces of cloth on the bottom hinge and some hair on the upper hinge. The Coroner : Your theory is that the old gentle- man fell against the door ? Witness : He must have fallen on the bottom hinge, while the top hinge caught his head. I gather that if you had kept straight on your road, you would have knocked both these men down ?—Yes. It was to avoid both of them that you took to your wrong side ?—Yes. And deceased followed you across the road ?—Yes. Witness added that he had been a driver about six years, had driven the car in question over 4,000 miles, and bad never had an accident before. _

Mr Roberts: These were two elderly gentlemen and , you had 200 yards in which to pull up. Why didn't you pull up sooner? Witness: I was pulling up all the time, and just as I came about level with them I had almost stopped. If you had stopped this would not have happened. Couldn't you have stopped ?—I could have stopped. Dr Jaxo, who was called to deceased when he was lying in the roadway, said the out on his head was one inch long and he was suffering from shook. With assistance the deceased walked home. At that time witness did not anticipate a fatal ending, but signs of cerebral hcemorrhage developed, and that was the cause of death. Deceased was quite blind in one eye and very deaf. It was more likely that the injury had been caused by the de:eased falling against the door of the car than by the car running into him. The Coroner said that in his view there was not sufficient evidence to place the driver on his trial for manslaughter. To justify that course, the jury would have to be satisfied that he was guilty of gross and culpable negligence. The whole of the evidence was against that. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death " rid exonerated the driver from all blame.

div.head: EARTH IN AN ENVELOPE.
div.p: THE EARTH IN AN ENVELOPE.

The world of ours floats through space wrapped up in an envelope and a very useful envelope it is. It is the thing we call the atmosphere. It may perhaps surprise some of you to know that we have yet to learn a great deal about the air. It is such a familiar thing that we seldom think about it ; yet all the world over from the equator to the arctic regions men of science are studying the atmosphere, and they are gradually gett- ing at the facts. We all know, of course, that the warm air immediately surrounding the earth is only a thin belt. In this thin layer we live and move. It is only about two miles thick. At this height the freezing-point is reached, and then for about six miles the temperature grows colder and colder until it reaches about 167 degrees below the freezing-point. In our own layer the air moves in all sorts of directions, in storms and swirls and cyclones. In the second or colder layer, this is not the case. The wind moves in great swirls caused by the spinning of the earth on its axis, and the current follows an easterly direction. The higher one goes, the more furious is the gale that blows. Then a curious thing is discovered. Above this second layer comes a third, and as soon as it is entered the temperature begins to rise. The higher up we go the warmer it gets, although it is still far below the freezing point. Here the wind does not follow the lead of the currents in the second layer, but blows any way. How far up this layer extends we do not know. Instruments have been sent up as high as 18 miles, and still they were in this layer. What is above that is still unknown, and we can only speculate as to how thick the envelope is.

div.head: HORSE'S PRAYER.
div.p: THE HORSE'S PRAYER.

"To thee, my master, I offer my prayer. Feed me, water and care for me, and, when the day's work is done, provide me with a shelter, a clean dry bed, and a stall wide enough for me to lie down in comfort. Be always gentle with me and talk to me. Your voice often means as much to me as the reins. Pet me sometimes, that I may serve you the more gladly and learn to love you. Do not jerk the reins, and do not whip me when going up-hill. Never strike, beat, or kick me when I do not understand what you mean, but give me a chance to understand you. Watch me, and if I fail to do your bidding, see if something is not wrong with my harness or feet.
Don't draw the straps too tight; give me freedom to move my head. If you insist on my wearing blinkers to keep me from look- ing round, at least see to it that they do not press against my eyes.
Don't make my load too heavy, and don't leave me tied up in the rain. Have me well shod.

Examine my teeth when Ido not eat. I may have an ulcerated tooth, and that you know is very painful. Do not tie my head in an unnatural position, or take away my best defence against flies and mosquitoes by cutting off my tail. _

I cannot tell you when I am thirsty, so give me pure cold water frequently. Do all you can to protect me from the sun; and throw a cover over me—not when I am working, but when I am standing out in the cold. Don't force an ice-cold bit into my mouth, but warm it first in some warm water or in your hand. _

I always try to do cheerfully the work you require of me : and day and night I stand for hours patiently waiting for you. An, finally, oh my master, when my uso-. ful strength is gone, do not turn me out to starve or freeze, or sell me to some cruel owner to be slowly tortured and starved to death; but do thou, my master, take my life in the kindest way, and your God will reward you ;here and hearafter. You may not consider me irreverent if I ask this in the name of Him who was born in a stable." This prayer, printed on card, has been posted up by order in Municipal stables both in New York City and Boston. OFF TO DREAMLAND. The Westminster Gazette a few weeks ago gave a clever little poem written by a child nine years old. Her name is Miss Ruth Vivian Phillips and liere are the verses :
Ho Boatman, Ho! We want to go To Dreamland over the seas. Pray tell us the way To get there to-day. And Boatman, please, What must we pay ?

" Six kisses you pay If you want to go To Dreamland, over the seas, you know. Six kisses you pay And I take you away To Dreamland, over the sunlit bay! Here! Boatman, here! Come near, come near, And take the price, though it is so dear. For we see it's clear We'll have to pay If we'd go to Dreamland, far away !
THIS WEEK'S STORY. HE FELT QUITE SAFE.

"Have you a good chauffeur, Bronson ? " asked Willoughby. "No, I haven't," said Bronson. "Only an old stupid gardener who doesn't know the first thing about machinery." "But, my dear fellow, aren't you afraid he'll break your neck ? " demanded Willoughby. " 0 no " said Bronson.

" What guarantee have you that he won't land you and your car in a ditch some day ?" said Willoughby. "Oh, he couldn't possibly do that," smiled Bronson. "Why not? " asked Willoughby. "Why, because I haven't any car," said Bronson.

div.p: INSURANCE DAY,
THE ACT WELCOMED AT A WARRINGTON PUBLIC MEETING.
REPLY TO MR. HAROLD SMITH'S CRITICISMS.

Monday last will go down to history as the cloy Co which Mr. Lloyd George's great scheme of national insurance came into opeiation. The occasion was fittingly celebrated in Wan ington by the holding of an open-air meetb,g near A rpley Station, under the joint auspices of :the Progressive Labour League and the Junior Liberal Association. 'I here was an excellent attendance and the enthu,i ism was a et, ik ing evidence of the failure of the Tory efforts to excite resentment egaimt this the greatest legislative achievement of our timn. Mr. PETER PEACOCK (chairman of the executive of the Liberal Art-oetation), who riresided, welcomed the Act as one who had taken a keen and active interest in friendly society work. Ile pointed nut that the friendly eocieties had been losing members at the rate of 250,000 a 3 ear. The efforts put forward to induce the people to make voluntary provision fir the inevitAble rilny day had not been successful. div.head: HOLIDAY IN DUBLIN
div.p: A HOLIDAY IN DUBLIN
AND SOME OF ITS ADVANTAGES.

The majority, of summer holiday makers in deciding on a place to visit as a rule make for some seaside resort such as Scarborough, Blackpool, the Isle of Man, or Margate, or Brighton, not many think of visiting Dublin as they regard it merely as a city I situated on the river Liffey, but as a matter of fact, there is no place within the United Kingdom which as a base for a most enjoyable and diversified holiday will compare with the capital of Ireland, far unlike most other cities it is within a short tramway ride cif a whole series of seaside resorts, which in regard to beauty of the surrounding scenery and fine seas are unrivalled If the northern holiday maker patronises Blackpool, it is true that he can visit Southport, Lytham, St. Amass- on-Sea, and cross to Morcarnbe, but all these plans bear a very close resemblance, one to the other, so far as the configuration of the surreunding seer ery is concrrned. This is not the ease in regard to the tourist who visias the Irish capital. Within the haundaries of 'he city itself, if he cares to remain there for two or three days he can see many buildings ot historic interest, such as Dublin Cantle, the old Parliament House, the Vice Regal ledge, the residence of the Lord Lieutenantpf Ire'and, Nttional Museum of Ireland, Four Courts &o, and it must be remem- bered that the air of the sity is quite clear, and ma smoke-laden like that of a manufacturing centre; but the city's strong recommendation to the holiday maker, especially coming from come of the I u-y smoky cities of the N rth of England, lies in the many different seaside spots which he tan visit during a brief stay, seeing something of interest in each radte umike anything he saw in the others. We will presume he, to begin with, puts up within the centre of the city, and near the we at Nelsen Column er cted by Gretton to con:Rueter,' ate the battle of Trafa'gar. LTaking a tram car from hero to Dolly mount he cat be iii an hour's time on ttie pier of a very p'easant spot where grand bathing may he enityrd, the sea I reuld this not bring deep. The place is better ki o vn as " Clewed," and is famous as the site on which a peat victory was obtained, in early history, over the invading Danes by one of the Irish Kings. The country around is hi'ly and beatrifully worded. The text day by 1 a little car ride he cin j uruey t Kingstown, visit 1 the fine harbour into which the Holyhead baste run, see King George IV.'s Monument, visit the Biaanical Garden and pars a my pleasant day. Another silent railway j urney born the city aid the holiday m iker will reach Bray, one of the prettiest spots of all arcurd Dubin, often called Bray Head ; here there is a fit e open tea, of which a good view can be got from the promenade, and, a very beautiful spot to which he I can welk wl ile here is called " The Dargle." Poth Kingstown at d Bray can boast of largo handsome hotels but the via tor ta either plaae can easi'y obtain his board for a day on reasonable terms, or stay there in the a me way, for that m Mee. Returning to Dublin he can take car the neat morning and so in arrive at another lovely spot called llowth, Lear wide!' is llowth Castle, the residence of Lord Talbot eta Malahide, and ljing cif the ccars‘ of which is a rocky island known as Ireland's Eye. The sea view here may be described as truly grand, and amongst the surrounding bills some most enjoy- able walks are to be f, mid, whilst taking which the tauriste' eye will fall on views f mountain mid sea, which in beauty it would be hard to turpass. In the evening on his return to Dubin he can, if he wishes, visit one of the thcatresahe Gaiety is the chief theatre, ar take a jaunting car, and enjoy a drive through the Phenix Park, ore of the largest parks in the United Kingdom...mill another p'ace which to visitor to Dublin should miss is Kifli ey, with its famous Lill and Castle, and Dalkey, off which lies Dalkey Island where the famous " Rocking Stone " can be a en ; this large boulder by a mere touch of the hand can be set la eking on its foundation in a manner which is very surprising. All these spots lie eking the coast-line, and it costs little to reach there by rail, or tram-car. Comfortable and clean apartments for ti.vo may be had at Bray for 265. a week with board. Within the city area there are, of course, many handsome, luxutious, and expen- eive hotels, such as the " Gresham " and "Inter- national." These are in Sackville-streot, and are for wealthy minims. Then there is the" Waverloy," near the O'Connell Monument, the tariff of ehieh is less, and in Marlborough-street (38) "The Ashbourre," a homely hotel of smaller dimenei ms, vi here visitors can get a good bedroom fir I Is. a week, and make any twins they like as to their board, according to what they require, all being cleanly and the attendance good. 'ibis, and a few other similar houses, will lie found to suit working reople, and are a good centre to stay at to reach all places of interest. Glasnevin Cemetery where lie buried Daniel O'Connell, Parnell and other notabilii les can easily be reached from het e and visitors can visit the coffin of the gre it Liberator, , see the replica of one of the old Irish Round Towers and the Batty Sullivan Memorial, whereas a holiday at Killarney might be expensive. Plenty of excursions ' tun there an the stammer months from Dublin, so a day can be spent there at a cost, for all, of about half a sovereign. Mat y pretty spots in Wicklow, such as the Vale of Avoca, ltathnow, Rathdrune, Wooden. bridge, and Arklon may also lo seen, at no great cost, and are well worth a v.sit.

'Jim sea air at all the sp its named is bracing, and the English visitor has the enjoyment of the voyage over to Irelaial, the fares f it. which sin cheap in the auminer time. If one journeys via Holyhead the railway journey is long, and only about four and a half hours are spent on the water. A lengthier stay on the sea may be obtained by going from Liverpool or sailing down the Manchester Ship Canal. Some very comfoitible boats take the last named route, and one can journey from the Manchester Decks, which are never so busy aud thronged as those at Liverpool, to the North Wall, Dublin, close to the Custom Manse, for about 10s. return salom, spending a good portion of the day on the open sea, Boats leaving Manchester at 12 o'cli ck mid-day, 'each the North Wall, Dublin, at 6 o'clock the following morning. The National Art Gallery in the city is another place whore a pleasant day can be spent, and a visit to Mcrrion and Rutland-squares in the city, which tnay be termed the 13ayswater ot Dublin, should not be missed. In Sackvitle-street are the Rotunda Buildings, the scene of many historic gatherings. A j aureey to the Corragh Camp dope not take long, and travelling by rail to Bray one passes the famous Leopards town race course. The people, generally, will be found very civil, obliging, and sober. In a thee weeks holiday spent in the neighbourhood the writer did not see a single street fight. In regard to jaunting car journeys, hotel accommodation rates. &c., the visitor if he fixes the terms beforehand will be safe nut to bs done; altogether, fee the reasons named, one may visit other places, at much more expense, see far less for his money, and enjoy less change of scene than if he visits Doblin. At Howth, are also the remains of an old Abbey. The tariff named for Bray refers, of course, to the smaller houses; the writer met a gentleman and bis wife on the boat returning, who said they had obtained very clean and comfortable apartments at Bray on these terms. The gentleman was a senior clerk in a large firm near Liverpool. At Dalkey ie a fort and garrison artillery, the; " Rocking Htene " is close to the former. A good fishing fleet goes out from Howth, and a long bi eak- water, along which tourists can walk, and provided with seats, stretches out into the sea in the direction ! of Ireland's Eye. Some very boisterous seas may be watched from the breakwater when the weather is rough. There are no very large hotels at Howth but a comfortable hostelry faces the sea, and in front of it is the Dublin tram terminus. One of the best walks here is up the hills at the back of this hotel. English visit ais sill be surprised to find many of the houses here, and some villas along the tram route, built on the flat, or bungalow,'system. The traveller by tramcar to most of the spots named covers a good part of the way passing along close by the sea, the roadwaya at many points being covered with the gsesp foliage of thp trees, and somewhat Manchester and Liverpool eteansers make their way to tbe Liffey pat, Clonlarf, and near the light- house, on the opposite side of the bay to the pier,is an almost solitary cottage, the light in which is the last thing passengers in the steamers see of habitation in their outward voyage. The English passenger s'eamers are commaccted by experienced seamen and it has hardly ever happened that life has been lest. One of the sites of .Dublin still to be named is the ancient St, Patrick's Cathedral, so closely associated with the noted Dean Swift, and another the famous Tr:nity College on College Green. Visitors may enter the quadrangle easily, and view the massive buildings of which the College is composed, and plessant gardens, with fountains and lakes, are to le found in Merricn and Rutland Squares. Numerous statues exist round College Green, the chief being those of Irish statesmen, and the large bronze gold-mounted

div.head: MR. R.. L. OUTHWAITE, M.P.
div.p: MR. R.. L. OUTHWAITE, M.P.

Mr. Outhwaite, the new Member for Hanley, is the son of an Australian farmer, and he spent his youth on sheep and cattle farms in Australia and New Zealand. He has fought two former elections. He con- tested West Birmingham against Mr. Chamberlain in 1906, an Horsham in January, 1910. _ _

div.head: YON TOE ELECHON WAS WON:
div.p: YON TOE ELECHON WAS WON:

Interviewed after the declaration of the poll, Mr. Outhwaite said :—" When I liest came doe n I said that I believed that we were on the eve of a very great advance on the question of land value taxation for the purpose of limiting monopoly control of the land. We hat been inf nmed that the Chancellor of the Exchequer with the co-op, ration of the Prime Minister, Ivas about to embark on a gre t campa'gn of freeing tl o laud. I made the text of rill my speeches the concluding words of Mr. Lloyd George's speech at Woodford Green, made two or three days before I addressed the Liberal Executive. I s tid I believed, just at this critical time, if the Chrucellor of the Exchequer had a mandate from a great democratic constituency such as this, it would have a powerful effect in influencing the Jovernment policy in this matter. All through the contest we had a large number of speakers from the land taxers group in the House of Commons, aided by those who are known throughout the country as exp: - or nts of the single-tax movement, c.mducting a c.im- reign in enCre conformity with the proposition which I had put before the electors at the start.

111 E LAND AND THE LOCALITY. "At the same time it his to he reopguised that Hanley is one of those districts which are peculiarly overburdened by the system of raising revenue for great national services such as education and poor relief by way of local rates. This has not born an irrational, theoretical propaganda. It has been some- thing coining right home to the people of this district. I put before the ratepayers the policy formulated in the memorial vthich has been presented to the Govern- ment on rating and taxation reform. That memorial suggested that certain services such as education, poor relief, police, main roads and asylums should be treated as national sr:l-vices aid financed from the Excliequrr. I vas able to show that were these proposals adopted there would be an enormoui relief to this distrit t, whose land values are low arid whose burdens are extraordinai fly high." As to the Liberal-Labour question Mr. Outhwaite said : "1 should certainly say this is a Liberal seat In supm rt of the Liberalism that I put before the electors. If the Government should repudiate this Liberalism, well this constituency, I should say, will repudiate the Government. The seat is Literal to-day because I said I confidently believed the Govern- risnt wee going to trop od along these lines and these prop: sa's proved to be more acceptable to the working men than those put forward by the many ebour. nnembers who came down to the constituency. They ridiculed the proposals of the land value taxers, cast aspersions on their honesty, and put forward their proposa's for land nationail,ation. We were able to pour ridicule upon the suggestion that we should buy out the landowners if Engiand, and our proposal that we 'should make a beginning by taxing the land found far more favour. I think in future it will be useless fcr any Liberal to ignore this question." THE INSURANCE ACT. Mr. Outliviaite 6 Med on the Insurance Act question : " I think if no great question had been raised, such as the land question, perhaps the small irritation that naturally exists in the adoption of some new policy might have affected the voters, but that was put into a secondary position. The people followed my view that we should regard the Insurance Act as en accomplished reform, and instead of theorising as to its defects should wait to see it in operation, and then get any necessary amendments carried out,"

Nominations were then takrn for the positions of D.C.R., and S.D.C.R , for next term. P.O It., Bro. T Roden was nominated for pJsition of D.O It.,aud P.C.R, Bro. S Healy as S.D.C.R. A discussion as to tbe position of the Oder under the Insurance Act led to many valuable suggestions being received for the benefit of the special committee which has been formed by the district to deal with all matters appertaining to the Act. The Delegates reportcd a large baths of members into their respective Courts under both voluntary and State sections. The D.C.R., Bro. Baines then closed the Court with the usual ritual of the Order.

div.head: Padgate.
div.p: Padgate.

MUSICAL SUCCESSES.—The following pupils of Miss Heath, L.V.C.M., passed very successfully at the recent examination of the Victoria College of Music, London :—Primary grade (piano), Miss Violet Lawton, 90 marks first class withlhonours, Miss Patti Churchill, 89 marks, first class with honours, both of Stockton _Heath, and Master Percy Starkey, King and Queen Hotel, 69 marks, first class pass.

div.head: Stockton Heath,
div.p: Stockton Heath,

HILL CLIFF} AND STOCKTON HEATH UNITED BAND OF IlorE.—ln oonnection with the above an open-air Temperance Meeting was held in Victoria-square, Stockton Heath, on Tuesday evening, when Mr Thomas D Leslie, the local agent of the United Kingdom Alliance, was the speaker. Mr Walter Twiss presided (in the absence of the Rev George Curtis), and was sup- ported by several well-known temperance workers. A number of Band of Hope children sang several temperance hymns, Master Ernest Whitfield accompany- ing on the harmonium.

div.head: Frodsham.
div.p: Frodsham.

YOUNG EXCURSIONIST'S DRUNKEN FREAK. At Frodsham Police Court on Monday, a youth, Arthur Bckwith, of Hunslet, Leeds, was fined .22 lis and costs for being drunk and disorderly and with interfering with the cnmfort of passengers, and also with doing wilful damage to a London and North- Western Railway carriage to the extent of £2 is. at Helsby last Saturday week. Alfred Peel, of East Ardsley, Leeds, a passenger on an excursion train returning from Llandudno to Leeds, said he was asked by the passengers in the prisoner's carriage to go and pacify him. Going along the corridor, he found him mad drunk and striking out in all directions. Two windows were broken, and witness with another passenger held him down till Helsby was reached. On being taken out there the prisoner broke another pane of glass with his foot. Prisoncr's father said his son bad had the drink given to him, and he was not responsible for what be did. His son had a good character previously. The prisoner also pleaded that the drink made him tot Ally uncon- scious of his actions.

div.head: Winwick.
div.p: Winwick.

ASSAULT AT THE ASYUT Al.—At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, otu Wednesday,Rohert Bardsley, of Pendleton, was summoned for assaulting Miss Tillett, a matron at the Winwick Asylum, and George Milner, an attendant. Mr. J. S. Francomb (law deck to the Winwick Asylum), said that on Saturday, June 22nd, the prisoner came to the asylum on a visit to his wife, who was an inmate. He refused to conform to the rules for visitors, and had to be escorted off the premises. While in the visiting-room he struck Miss Tillett on the arm, and when Milner was assisting him to leave he kicked him on the leg. The defendant was fined 20s. and costs, or fourteen days, in each case, the entence to run concurrently. ANNUAL SPORTS.—The annual sports for the attendants, nurses and patients of the County Asylum, were held on Thursday afternoon, commencing at 2.30 and finishing at 6 o'clock. The weather was all that could he desired, and the sports were quite up to their usual standard, some very interesting and exciting events being witnessed. At the close of the programme Mr. Mercer presented the prizes to the fortunate ones. Others present were :—Dr. Simpson (superintendent of the Institute) and his staff, Alderman Evans (Warring- ton), Aldermen Taggart and Roberts (Liverpool). The Institute Orchestra played selections under the leader- ship of Mr. Haines.

div.head: Penketll.
div.p: Penketll.
PENKETH AND DISTRICT ROSE AND SWEET PEA SOCIETY.

The above society held their fourth annual exhibition of roses and sweet peas on Saturday at 3 o'clock in the afternoon at the Council School, Stocks-lane. The weather being fine, a good company gathered together for the opening ceremony, which was kindly undertaken by Mrs. Dodds, president of the society. The Presi- dent, in her usual pleasing style, made a short speech, and remarked that although life was such a rush and people had little or no time to become enthusiastic yet she was glad to know that the success of the society was due to enthusiasts. (Applause.) She thought that the women should have half the praise for the success of the show. (Applause.) The number of entries was so large that the school was too small for all the exhibits. An orchestra under the direction of Mr James Watts, played selections during the afternoon and evening, dancing taking place in the evening. The Penketh Pierrot Troupe gave entertainments at intervals which were much enjoyed. The refreshments were in the capable hands of Miss ' Dumbill, Mesdames Aldoroft, Carrington, Dumbill, liampson, Waine, and Woods. Much credit is due to the work of the committee and Mr C Dumbill fot the success of the show.
