div.head: MANHOLE TRAGEDY AT MANCHESTER.
div.p: MANHOLE TRAGEDY AT MANCHESTER.

- - A Manchester Corporatian electrician, George Henry Gibson (56), of 1, Frederick-place, Rochdale-road, Manchester, WAS eloctrocuted while working in a man- hole near the Failsworth Pole. A workmate who was standing at the entrance of the manhole heard the deceased cry out, and on descending he found Gibson holding on to a live wire. The work- mate, grabbing hold of the deceased's clothes, pulled him away from the wire, but when he was removed from the manhole life was extinct.
The Examiner, Saturday, July, 20, 1912.

be as good a man as he was when he went away. He wished to thank the Council for the great kindnesses they had extended to him during his illness. He had to report one case of diptheria at Lower Stratton and a case of scarlet fever at Frodsham. In each case the necessary precautions had been taken. lhe report aas adopted. The next meeting of the Council will be heid on August 13th. RUNCORN MOTOR FATALITY. CHAUFFEUR NOT .TO BLAME.

The Ear of Ellesmere's chief chauffeur (W. E. Ballard) was freed from any blame by a Runcorn jury on Tuesday night, at the inquest on Owen Henry Dunne the eight-year-old son of a tailor, who was killed by a motor-car on Monday evening in Bridge-street. Ballard was driving Lord Ellesmere's chief cashier and three other men from a rent audit at Wilson's Hotel, and said he was travelling up Delph Bridge on a low gear, at not more than eight miles an hour, when the accident happened. A four-wheeled van was coming down the bank, and noticing children hanging behind it he sounded his horn twice. As quick as a stone from a sling "the deceased child darted from behind toe van and in the front of the car, and the off mudguard struck it on the bead. Witness pulled up in a couple of feet, but when the child was taken to Dr. Brunton's surgery it was dead, its skull being broken. Half a dozen witnesses said the car was being driven , carefully. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and it was said the Earl of Ellesmere would pay the funeral expenses. FREEMEN OF WIDNES. TWO VETERAN TOWNSMEN HONOURED.

. _ There was a large gathering of councillors and prominent townspeople at Widnes Town Hall on Tues- day, when two honoured Widnesians received the free. dom of the borough at the hands of the Mayor (Alder- man F Neil). Resolutions had been passed at the December and February meetings deciding unanimously to mark the town's appreciation for strenuous services rendered by Major J W Wareing and Mr H Wade Deacon, by granting to them the highest honour at the disposal of the council. The chamber was decorated tastefully with flower', and the beautiful caskets attracted much attention. The relatives of the recipients attended in numbers, chief among them being Mr Stuart Deacon (stipendiary magistrate of Liverpool) and Mrs Wareing. The caskets containing the resolutions of the Town Council were of sterling silver richly gilt. In addition to bearing photographs of the recipients, they also have panels of miniatures in colour of the Technical Schools, Town Hall, Transporter Bridge and Victoria Park. In the case of Major Wareing, the casket is surmounted by a figure symbolical of •` Justice," and Mr Deacon by a figure representing "Knowledge," To the plinth. on which the casket stands, is attached a plate bearing the inscription of the date of presentation and the autographs of the Mayor and Town-clerk. Major Wareing has been associated with the public affairs of the town for 40 years, and, in addition to having been twice mayor, he has also filled the office of chairman of the Prescot Board of Guardians. He has been a member of the Town Council since the incorpora- tion of the borough, and was a member previously of the old Local Board, A member of the Widnes School Board, he subseqently served on the Education Com- mittee. He rendered most important service to the town in its progress and advancement. Mr. H. Wade Deacon has been identified prominently with the educational progress of the borough, and, with a view to encouraging and stimulating the cause of higher education in the town, he founded recently in the University of Liverpool a valuable scholarship, known as the "Henry Wade Deacon Scholarship," which is tavailable for students from the Widnes Secondary School. He was instrumental largely in securing the adoption of the Free Libraries Act in Widnes in 1985, and has acted since continuously as chairman of the Free Library Committee.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

INSURANCE ACT CELEBRATION. "MEAN OPPOSITION." An open-air meeting of very large dimensions was held in the Victoria-square, Widnes, on Saturday even- ing, in celebration of the advent of the NationaC Insurance Act. Mr J B Aitken (president of the Vvidnes Division Liberal Association) presided, and said it was a great day in the history of the country, for the Act, whose passing into law they were celebrating, would do more for the great body of the people of the country than any Parliamentary Act passed in his time,, and he had been a politician for 50 years. He moved a resolu- tion congratulating his Majesty's Ministers " upon the inauguration of so great a measure of social reform as the National Insurance Act, and condemns the mean and insidious methods of opposition to it employed by the Tory party and Press. Continuing, Mr Aitken asked," Why should the Tories imagine that the Act was not going to be successfully put into operation. The truth was that the Tories were greatly disappointed that they therflsel yes had not passed the Act They had talked long about old-age pensions, and also insurance, but they never attempted to bring any such measures in the House of Commons. Mr T Ashley seconded, and Mr J B Martindale (Manchester) supported the resolution, which was carried.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr. J. Spruce, presiding. CHILDREN'S HOME. The Clerk reported that at a meeting of the Children's Home Committee on the Bth July the committee interviewed the agent of the premises who agreed to recommend that the agreement be come to with the owner. The committee recommended that the tender of Messrs J G Davies and Co., of Frodsham amounting to £753 10s, be accepted. The Chairman said he was sorry that the amount named was in excess of what they had anticipated. The expectations of the architect had been exceeded and he hoped that when it was carried out it would prove satisfactory to all. (Hear, hear). He moved that the Council accept the recommendation. Mr Morris seconded and the proposition was carried. INSURANCE. The Parliamentary Committee recommended that all employees of the Board in receipt of less than £l6O per year be insured under part one of the Insnrance Act. That would practically include all officers of the Board. Mr Woodward in moving the adoption of the minute, said the committee were of the opinion that it was the easier and safer course to take on behalf of the Board. (Hear, hear). Mr T Wright seconded and the minute was carried. FIL CHY AND VERMINOUS PRISONERS. The Clerk read the following letter from Superin- tendent Ennion of Runcorn:—The attention of the Secretary of State has been directed to a public nuisance attributable to the fact that filthy and verminous prisoners are sometimes conveyed by the police in a cab or by rail to the Court where they might be charged 'lnd from the Court to prison.He desired to be informed whether arrangements could be made by the police with the Poor Law authorities for the cleansing at workhouses or casual wards of any verminous prisoner who might be brought there by the police for that purpose. It would, of course, be understood that cleansing would only take place in the case of prisoners whose condition constituted a serious annoyance and possible danger to the public ; that the police would be responsible for taking the prisoners to and from where the cleansing apparatus was available, and that prisoners would remain in the custody of the police curing the cleansing process. He desired to know whether the Board were prepared to undertake to cleanse prisoners in the custody of the police and on what terms, if any. At a meeting of the Visiting Committee it was resolved that the Clerk be instructed to write pointing out that the Guardians had not thn proper conveniences to undertake the proposal. it was also decided that Mr. Morris and the Master interview Mrs. A. Griesdale of Birkenhead and if they were satisfied, to recommend her for the position of nurse at the institution. In proposing the adoption of the minutes Mr. Morris said they had decided that they were not in a position to entertain the application of the police at all. In the first instance the clothes would have to be in the store for at least 12 hours and they would have to provide the prisoners with other clothes in the meantime. In regard to the applications for the position of nurse they had had two replies. Those who had read Dickens would recollect Sam Weller said " Bevare of Vidders " but they were thinking of trying one this time. (Laughter). She might stop longer than the others. A Voice : Are you going to interview her ?—Yes. Mr. Linaker (jun.) Bevare of the Vidders then. (Laughter.) The next meeting of the Guardians twill be held on August 13th. RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday. Mr. Linaker presiding. A QUESTION OF LIABILITY. Mr C L Evans wrote complaining that a stone wall in Summer-lane' Halton (the road leading from the Norton Arms toAstmoor Bridge) was coming down and he contended that it was the Council's business to repair this. Mr. J. Swinton, surveyor to the Council, expressed the opinion that the Council did not erect the wall nor did he think it had been erected by any previous highway authority or repaired by any. Mr. Evans had admitted that the estate had repaired the walls previ- ously but be thought that the Highway Authority was liable by law to maintain such walls which held up the land above the level of the high Arty as in this case in which the land was four or five feet above the road. The Clerk said that he bad written denying the liability and the Council approved of his action. GRAPPENHALL SEWAGE SCHEME. The minutes of the Grappenhall, Latchford Without, and Tholwall Sewage Committee stated that the engineer had explained that a difficulty had arisen in connection with the purchase of the land of Admiral Jones Parry which was required for the sewerage out- fall and purification works and he recommended that the whole site belonging to Admiral Jones Parry, and consisting of about 14 acres be purchased for the Wm of £1,050. It was resolved that the recommendation of the engineer be adopted and that a provisional agreement be entered into for the purchase of this site. The Clerk reported that he had considered the question of the apportionment ot the expenses of the construc- tion of so much of the works AS would be for the com- mon benefit of the parishes included in the scheme. He had ascertained that in a recent order issued by the Local Government Board the number of buildings proposed to be served by the scheme was taken as a basis of appor- tionment and that the order provided for the adjust- • ment of the apportionment every five years based on the number of buildings at that time connected with the scheme. He also submitted a statement of the number houses proposed to be connected with the scheme and apportiknments of the costs of the works. There were 389 houses in Grappenhall., 150 in Latchford, 87 in Thelwall, total 626. The total cost of outfall works land with outfall sewer from the site of the outfall works to the boundaries of Thelwall and Grappenhall, and to be apportioned between the three parishes was £10.250. This was apportioned as follows :—Grappenhall, £6,369 ; Latchford Without, £2,456; Thelwall. £,1425. The total cost of outfall sewers connected ivith the two parishes of Grappenhall and Latchford Without,and the parish of Thelwall was £2,657. The apportionment on Grappenhall was £1,917, and on Latchford Without £740. The total cost of subsidiary sewers to be charged separately to the sec:mint of the parishes actually served—Grappenhall, £3,478 ; Latchford With- out, £872 • Thelwall, £1,243. The summary of charges against each of the parishes concerned was as follow. : Grappenball, .£11,764 ; Latchford Without, £4,068 ; Thelwall, £2,668. The total estimated cost of the scheme was £18,500. It was resolved that it be a recommendation to the District Council (1) That the number of buildings pro- posed to be served by the scheme be taken as the basis of apportionment of the cost of the works as will be for the common benefit of the three parishes ; (2) that a like basis be taken for the apportionment of the cost of works connected with the parishes of Grappenhall and Latchford Without ; (3) that the apportionments be adjusted every five years, bared on the number of buildings at the time connectei with the scheme ; (4) that the figures prepared by the clerk be adopted and that the notice of apportionment be served on the overseers of each parish concerned. Mr G Pilling, as chairman of the committee, in moving the adoption of the minutes said he would not say he did so with a great amount of pleasure because it was a serious matter for the parishes concerned, but he did so because he supposed it was a matter that would be done if not at the present time, some time sooner or later. They had made a good bargain in securing about 7j-F acres of land for £360 whereas £750 had previously been paid for a similar area of land. (Applause). Mr Hallows seconded and the motion was carried. WALTON INKERIOR SEWERAGE. The Walton Inferior Sewage Committee reported that the committee had inspected the flushing tank near the Walton Mill Pool and the joint of intake of the drain pipe which supplies the flushing tank with water from the mill stream. It was resolved that the District Council be recommended to write Messrs J White and Co. agents to the Halton estate asking per- mission to raise the height of the weir near the joint of the side intake and to construct a small chamber round the inlet of the pipe. The Council agreed to act as the committee suggested. THE BRINE BILL. The Salt Union wrote cordially thanking the Rural Council for the valuable assistance given in supporting the opposition to the Brine Pumping Bill. The action taken by the Council was none the less appreciated from the fact that the Council, like the Salt Union, had considerable interests at stake. THE MEDICAL OFFICER. div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

ART AT ST. HELENS. The Mayor of St. Helens (Alderman Sir Yoseph Beecham) opened on Wednesday an interesting exhibi- tion of the works of students attending the St. Helens School of Art at the Gamble Institute. The exhibition is being held at the Museum in Victoria Park, and has been arrangad by Mr John Skeaping, the art master 4 It consists of oil paintings, water-colours, specimens of stained glass with designs and pictures, clay modelling, drawings from life and from casts, lithography, and original sketches. _ . . . .

Sir Joseph Beecham, who had come specially from London to open the exhibition, said every artist, how- ever great his fame in after life,had to have a beginning and the work they saw before them was Of interest, because it was that of students of the town. A great deal of it was much better than he had expected to find, and he hoped the Art School would prosper and that the work shown would encourage other students to go in and try what they could do. div.head: DEATH OF A NOTED WESLEYAN . PHILANTHROPIST.
div.p: DEATH OF A NOTED WESLEYAN . PHILANTHROPIST.

The death hss occurred att-itls--rr;sicience in London after a long illness, of the Rev Dr Stephenson, founder of the National Children's Home. It was in the neighbourhood of the notorious New Cut, Lambeth, that the doctor's lifework among friendless and orphan children was begun in 1868. A small house was taken in Church-street, Waterloo-road, and four homeless lads received into it during the first week. In a short time a second larger house had to be rented, a stable at the back being transformed into a dining-room, and a hay- loft over it into a dormitory. From this humble beginning Dr. Stephenson developed the National Children's Home and Orphanage as it exists to-day, comprising the headquarters in London, and the thirteen branches in this country and Canada. In 1873 Dr. Stephenson was appointed the first principal of 'the home and orphanage his efforts had founded, and for twenty-seven years he devoted all his energies to the establishment and extension of the great philan- thropic enterprise. At the end of that period, acting upon medical advice, he retired from the principalship, to which the late Dr. Arthur Gregory succeeded, and undertook a pastoral charge at Ilkley.

BATHERS ELECTROCUTED IN A POND. BERNE, WEDNESDAY. A, strange accident has caused the death of three lads who were bathing in a pond in the neighbourhood of an electrically driven mill at Kriegstetten, in Canton Soleure. In some not yet explained way a strong electric current went through the water, and with a terrible cry the three Youths were submerged and instantly killed. Many dead fish were also di:covered in the pond L afterwards.

div.head: NON-INTOXICATING BEER.
div.p: NON-INTOXICATING BEER.
ST. HELENS BREWER'S UNFORTUNATE ENTERPRISE.
Sequel to a Warrington Prosecution.

In the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court on Monday, before Mr. Registrar Cooper, the vicissitudes of a brewer in attempting to introduce a non-intoxicating beer were related by the sufferer, Henry Finlay, of Sutton, St. Helens. He appeared for public examina- tion upon a statement of affairs showing liabilities of £451 13s Id, and assets (mostly shares in the Phcenix Brewery, of which he was manager) valued at £443 3s 6d. The debtor attributed his position to a prosecution by the Excise authorities in respect of a patent non- intoxicating beer, and the costa of an unsuccessful appeal by him as patentee to the Court of King's Bench. Asked as to this litigation the debtor said he had taken out a patent for the production of a non- intoxicating beer, but having the taste and character of ordinary beer. The Official Receiver : Your idea was this beer could be sold by anybody without a licence? The Debtor said that was so. The idea was to keep within the 2 per cent, of alcohol which he had under- stood the law allowed to be sold without a licence. However, one of your customers was proceeded against by the Excise authorities ?—Yes ; it came before the Warrington magrstrates. The prosecution stated it had the appearance of beer and tasted like beer, and they said it was beer. They admitted it did not contain more than 2 per cent, of proof spirit, and the law, as I have understood it, says an Excise licence is not required for beer when it does not contain more than 2 per cent, of proof spirits. But the magistrates convicted, and fined the man £lO and costs ? The Debtor said an apneal was taken to the Court of King's Bench, which he financed, lie thought he ought to "see his customer through." The appeal came before the Lord Chief Justice and tw other judges, and the result was they upheld the magistrates' decision, The prosecution was, he thought, unjust, because there never had before been a prosecution for selling without e licenee when the beer did not contain more than 2 per cent, of proof spirit. The Official Receiver.—Well, the King's Bench seems to have found it was well conceived. The Debtor said, of course, he was not in a position to take the case further; but he still disputed the judgment. Continuing, the Debtor said be put the whole case before the Chancellor of the Exchequer, who did not even acknowledge the letter ; also the secretary of the company had communicated with the Board of Customs and Excise, but that letter also had been ignored. Amongst his creditors were two firms of solicitors who had acted in the matter. To one of them, before pro- ceeding with the defence, he had put the question: "If we lose this case and decide to appeal, what do you think it will cost ?” The solicitor said. It will cost you about £3O to appeal." "Oh," said the debtor, "I can stand that. We will appeal against it if we lose the case." As a matter of fact, added the debtor, it ran into close on £3OO. The debtor was examined on some other matters after which an adjournment was taken to Aagust 12.

div.head: FIRST MATERNITY BENEFIT.
div.p: FIRST MATERNITY BENEFIT.

Mr. Harold Spender related to the Fulham Liberals a story of how the Chancellor of the Exchequer con- tributed to the first maternity benefit paid in connec- tion with the National Insurance sc)ieme. Mr. Lloyd George was dining the other day with a few friends when news came that one of the Insurance Commis- sioners had been presented with s son. It was sug- gested that as the Commissioner would shortly have to dispense the maternity benefits to others, it would be appropriate for him to be the first recipient. Mr. Lloyd George immediately fell in uith the suggestion, and the diners had a whip round for the 305., the Chancellor contributing one-tnird of the amount. The sum was inserted in an envelope and forwarded to the Commissioner with the kind regards of the author of the National Insurance Act.

owley Bridge—A Suggestion. Sir,—lt was with the greatest pleasure, on my visit to the Old English Fair, that I found by inspection that a suspension foot bridge was being made over the river Mersey at the cost of the Corporation. This bridge will, undoubtedly, be of great advantage, nniting to a larger extent the inhabitants of Latchford, Howley and the Padgate district. Might I so far pre- trams to suggest to the Corporation that even with this great improvement, that Stockton Heath and district have yet to journey to Bridge Foot in order to take advantage of the new bridge, and I do not think it would he impossible for the Corporation to re-open the road underneath the London and North-Western Railway& Company's line, which commences on the Stockton Heath side at Lurchers-lane, and comes out slightly to the right of the Old Warps entrance. This road would be a great boon to the inhabitants of Stockton Heath. An annual payment as a trespass rent would place the London and North-Western Railway Company in a secure position.—Yours faith- fully, C. 1). PARKINSON. Bewsey Chambers, Warrington, • July 18th 1912.

div.head: Summering of Horses.
div.p: The Summering of Horses.

you allow me to make a practical suggestion with regard to the sua,mering of horses? There seems to be an established idea that horses can be turned out for the summer, and that providing they have sufficient grass and water, they require nothing else. My belief is different, and my practice is this: During the heat of the day, and so long as the flies are troublesome, I bring my horses in at 9 a.m, and keep them stabled till 6 p.m., turning them out again for the night. They have only one small feed at mid-day, and yet they keep in capital condition and ,are ready for work when required. It is certainly unwise to leave horses and livestock out in the full heat and sunshine, as the irritation caused by the flies keeps them constantly on the move and the force exerted by constant kicking, biting, stamping and stampeding, is very considerable indeed and is just so much waste of strength which ought to be avoided. I know of a case where a cart mare was turned out for the whole of last summer in some 20 acres of meadowland, on the level coast near Chichester, which Sir Rider Haggard says is the richest pasture in the Kingdom. This mare might have been expected to improve under t'..ese conditions, but by the Autumn she was absolutely nothing but skin and bone for which state it was admitted by the owner the flies had been responsible.—! am &c.,
W. J. C. NORRIS, Animals) Friend Society. Thakeham, Pulborough, July 10th.

div.head: Mr. H. Smith M.P. and the Fair.
div.p: Mr. H. Smith M.P. and the Fair.

Sir.—l should feel obliged if you would kindly allow me through the medium of your paper to thank the thousands of people who attended the Old English Fair last week and also the many kind friends who assisted to make the affair such a success. It would be utterly impossible fGr me to thank all individually. The Committee generally and the assistants worked most nobly and I rejoice to think that the Million Penny Fund is now closed. The only regret I have is that you should have criticised the absence of the local Member of Parlia- ment from the proceedings on the Thursday. As long as I have the honour to be connected with the Infirmary I shall never allow any question of politics to enter into any proceedings that I am interested in, as the work is done by people of all shades of political feeling and religion and Mr. H. Smith was asked to come as the Member for the Borough. Unfortunately for us be was engaged on a law case and the following letter from him clearly gives the reason. July Bth. Dear Mr. Smethurst, I have bad news. I'm afraid there is no chance of my being present on Thursday. I have an important case on, which is being fixed for that day as a matter of convenience to Parties and Counsel concerned. This is most unfortunate but lam afraid it cannot be avoided in a profession such as mine. I hope my absence will not cause any inconvenience and that you will have very successful results.

Yours sincerely, (Signed) HAROLD SMITH. Surely that is quite sufficient. We know Mr. Smith is a professional gentleman who attends to his business, and everyone admires the hard work he puts in. Yours truly.
JAMES H. SMETHU RST.

div.head: Infirmary, Warrington, 18th July 1012.
div.p: The Infirmary, Warrington, 18th July 1012.
Orange Outrages.

Sir,—The most noticeable feature of the attitude of the Tory press, both locally and generally during the past ten days, has been thej significant silence in respect to the recent outbursts of Orange rowdyism and terrorism in Belfast and neighbourhood. Of course, it is quite natural that they should refrain from making public the logical results of the rebellious and disloyal political outbursts of Boner Law, Carson, F H Smith and Co. The orange rowdies of Belfast have interpreted their invective in the only possible manner. They have advanced on all their previous performances by distributing their attentions over every individual whom they suspected of holding demcoratic sympathies Liberal, Labour and Socialist toilers being equally persecuted with the long-suffering Catholic Nationalist. The 1,500 Catholics and 500 Protestants who were afraid to go to their work in the shipbuilding yards of Belfast must have peculiar opinions of the kind of loyalty and liberty which is masquerading under the Orange banner whose members are at the same time asserting that under Home Rule the Protestant religion will be persecuted. During the past week,l have had some very interesting conversations with a young Warrington mechanic of demccratic ideas, who has been for some months in the employ of Messrs. Harland and Wolfe, Belfast. This young man was warned on the Tuesday week preceeding the "glorious 12th," that his person was in danger and that it would be to his advantage if he went home for the " holidays." He decided that discretion was the better part of valour under the circumstances, and together with many others, left Belfast later in the week fur borne. To this young man, leaving England with profound Protestant convictions, the tactics of the Orange Lodges were unspeakably dis- gusting. He was an unwilling eye-witness of the gross maltreatment of scores of his fellow workers, many of whom were attacked singly, kicked and mutilated until it was necessary for the ambulance to intervene, the few Harbour policemen being helpless. Others leaving their work in boats were subjected to the hot fusilades of that favourite ammunition of the Orange man, the boiler rivet, still worse even being the thing of rifles at a Nationalist party returning by road from Maghery on Sunday, July 7th. My friend vows that to be thrown in the dock was not uncommon and he bitterly complains of the inadequacy of police on Queen's Island, where 20,000 men are employed. If any further substantiation is required. the 2,000 persons who assembled in the City Hill on July Bth and demanded military protection undoubtedly furnished it. Messrs. Harland and Wolfe recognised the seriousness of the situation aud the heinousness of this Orange Reign of Terror by threatening to close their works indefinitely. This, however, did not deter the "loyal" procession lets when parading the streets on the 12th from breaking hundreds of windows and attacking newspaper offices, business premises, churches and private houses. They inflicted injuries on many defenceless people, some having to receive hospital treatment and be confined as in-patients. It has been said that Hiberians were the instigatcrs in attacking a Sunday school party, a libel which was effectively disposed of by the Irish Chief Secretary in the House of Commons. On the contrary the Orange outrages commenced near Lisburn on June 25, and evidently have all been a pre-arranged scheme, which has completely failed owing to the good sense and better judgment of the law-abiding Catholic Nationalists and other demo- crats who know so well the shallowness of the Orange ease and the insincerity of the Orange and Tory leaders. These men and not their dupes must be held re- sponsible.—Yours truly,
DISGUSTED.

On their return the happy couple will take up residence at 107 London Road, Stockton Heath. div.head: Warren—Taylor.
div.p: Warren—Taylor.

A. pretty wedding was solemnized at Grappenhall Church on Tuesday morning, the contracting parties being Mr. E. Walter Warren, the eldest son of Mr. and Mrs J. E. Warren Wilderspool Causeway, and Miss Laura Rachel Taylor, the youngest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. E. Taylor also of Wilderspool Causeway,both well-known in local circles. The bride, who was given away by her father, was charmingly sttire.d in a dress of ivory liberty satin trimmed with silk lace, the train ornamented with orange blossoms, lovers' knots and pearls. She also wore a wreath and veil, the only ornament being a handsome pearl necklet, the gift of her mother. The bride was attended by three bridesmaids, Miss Taylor sister of the bride,who wore a dress of pale blue ninon-de-soir with Greek embroidery, Miss Evelyn Lawton and Miss Olive H. Gleave of Liverpool) nieces of the bride, who wore dresses like the bride, and gold signet rings the gifts of the bride-groom The service was conducted by the Rector (the Rev. Harry V. Pigot). The duties of best man were ably performed by Mr Duncan Cowdell (of Manchester),l while Mr. W. Percy Taylor, brother of the bride, performed the duties of groomsman. During the arrival and departure of the bridal party, Mr Shacklady rendered suitable music on the organ, while a merry peal was rung on the bells as the party left the church. The reception was afterwards held at the Hall Cafii, Stockton Heath. Later in the day the happy couple left for the Lake District where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride travelled in a navy costume with hat to match. They were the recipients of a large number of useful presents.

div.head: SECONDARY SCHOOL.
div.p: SECONDARY SCHOOL.
ANNUAL DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES. MORE ABOUT THE SHORTAGE OF TEACHERS.

To the scholars cf the Warrington Municipal S.contlary School the annual prize distribution is the red letter day cf the year, sod there was the usual happy gathering in the Borough Gymnasium on Tnursday afternoon, when the Mayor (Councillor Dr Joseph) presented the awards gained dating the:past year. It was pleasant to note the increasing interest in the work of the school, as evidenced by the large attendance of parents and friends of the scholars. lii addition to the formal procedure, there was a well- varied musical and dramatic programme, and the function was in every respect a gratifying success. In the absence cf Councillor H Roberts (chairman of the Education Committee), the chair was occupied by Mr Alfred J Jolley (deputy chairman), who was comiianied on the platform by the Mayor, Councillors T Birtles and W H J Jenkins, Mr E Plinston, Mr J Moore Murray (direct .r of education), Mr E S A Robson (principal) and Miss Clarke (senior mistress). It w's announced that letters of apology for non- attendance had been received from Councillor H Roberts and Mr Hnrold Smith, M.P. EDUCAIION SCHEME INCOMPLETE. THE ATTITUDE OF THE RATEPAYERS.

The CHAIRMAN extendeci;varn7;;;;;Cul-aireens to Mr Robson on the completion of another of the long series of years of work, faithfully and honourably rendered, in the interests of education ia Warrington, by himself personally. Neither Mr Robson, the mem- bers of the staff, nor the members of the Education Committee would dream of supposing that they always succeeded in giving complete and entire satisfaction to everybody. They could not hope to, if they did their duty honestly, but be ventured to say with complete confidence tont Mr Robson and his staff deserved to be publicly thanked for their loyal Beryl° 29. (Applause.)The parents of the students were to be con- gratulated on the fact that their sons and daughters had opportunities which they themselves were no fortmi- ate enough to enjoy In tneir earlier years—a fact which some of them looked back upon with regret and envy, if not with less satisfactory feelings. The Secondary School was absolutely second to none, s ) far as its building and equipmeht were concerned, that could be found in any town of anything like equal size—in fact be did not know of any town with four times the popu- lation of Warrington which had such a well-equipped school. It was desirtble that tha facilities should be appreciated and full tiAe made of them. The Secondary School, however, was only part of a large scheme for the development of edmiation. He very much regretted to say that the filing in of the further details of the btu-lawn scheme drawn up bed been practically at a Irtandstill. An impartial critic might ask : " How is it that although a very admirable skeleton scheme was submitted to the iiJard of Education nine years ago, only a snail fraction of the work sketched out in it has been completed ? " The real answer was Visa unfortuntrely
THE AJORITY OF THE R ATEPA VERS THOUGHT MORE

• ABOUT THE COST than of the true value of education and, from motives uf economy and fear of inducting expense, the full development of the original scheme had been delayed, although not dropped. He hoped that in due course tne outlines of the scheme would be filled.in and that instead of having, as at present, a more or lesi frag- mentary scheme they would have a symmetrical, well th iugh-out ant complete scheme of elementary and nigher education lu lull operation in the town. Before that could ba done they w iuld have to educate public opinion to the fact that one of the best investments was t ie improvement of the education of the rising genera- tion. (Applause). THE PRINCIPAL'S REPORT. DURATION OF SCHOOL LIFE ON THE INCREASE. _ _ .

The Principal preseuted his report as follows :—The number of pupils attending the Secondary School during the session 1911-12 has been 217, viz. :-120 girls and 97 boys compared with 227 last year, there using 122 girls sod 105 boys. There have also been in a tendance 15 student teachers, which is the same number es last year. There were 95 applications for admission and 63 of these entered the school. It is pleasing to is ite th,t

THE DE'RATION OF SCHOOL LIFE Is ON THE INCREASE, being now exactly three years and tour months. Of the 65 pupils leaving during the session, 30 are leaving at the end of the 2nd year, 17 at the end of the 3rd year, 4 at the end of the 4th year sod 15 bursars at the end of the sth year. I have to notify four changes in the staff, viz :—Mr B. El itlbety, M.Sc., Physics and Second Master, after eight years service in the school, was appointed bead master of the Earlestown Technical School ; MiS3 E M Congdon, 8.A., received a well-merited promotion to the Comae Secondary School ; Mr F Lord, M.Sc , is now engaged as engineering master at the Keighley Trades and Grammar School ; while Miss B Da wso,r, 8.A., reigned her post as senior French mistre.ss upon the occasion of her marriao. I feel sure that the I pupils, parents, and colleagues on the stall, will view I :be departure of these with regret and will appreciate the value of their bervices in building up the reputation of the school. (Applause.) The committee have filled up the vacancies by the eippAntment of Mr.) S Broome, M.Sc. of Manchester Univeraity, whose wide experience in boys' and girls' Sec-inch:try Schools has qualified him , for the important position of second master, of Miss C 'Morris B A Liverpool University, of Miss M Jolley, B.Sc., Liverpool University (one of our old pupils) and Mr N E France, M.Sc., Manchester University. With regard to the

ALTERATIONS IN THE SCHOOL CURHICUL UM, I have occasion to note the reorganization of the teaching in geography with its special practical work; the further development of oral French work together with the correspondence with pupils in French Secondary Schools and the extended curriculum of the art training. Parents will no doubt be interested to learn how tha special needs for the training of girls have been con- sidered and they will be glad to be reassured on this important point. Special work in biology is now done by girls in the 3rd and 4th years and extensions in the curriculum for domestic science (including cookery and art needlework) have also been taught to the pupils. The drill classes for girls are now in charge of the senior mistress, the boys' classes being taken by the Director of the Gymnasium. An interesting feature in the manual training work during the past session has been the construction of scientific apparatus by the buys under the direction of Mr Marshall and those parents present to-day who have the opportunity of seeing the exhibit will fully appreciate the importance of such a trainingifrom an educational point of view. lam glad to report that the social side of tbe school has been very successful as usual, for in addition to the ordinary athletic sports we have developed a Literary and Debating Society and a Morris dancing class, while the success of the boys' Whit week camp at Prestatyn under the superintendence of Mr. Broome showed that its extension to other parts of the country might reasonably be considered in future years. As to the examinations, the resultt printed on the pro- gramme will speak for themselves, but I should like to draw your attention to the continued successes of our old pupils. Three of them have advanced a further academic step in post graduate study :—Edith Isaac, M.A., Percy F. Boardman, B.So. (Honours) and Fred R. Jolley M.Sc. (Tech), while we have two new graduates, viz. :—Dorothy Johnson, B.A. (Liverpool) and Elsie Swaine, B.A. (Manchester). It is gratifying to note that parents are taking a much keener interest in _ _ _

CHOOSING -CAREERS for their sons and daughters, and they are finding that a sound Secondary school education is an open passport in the broad fields of labour. It is a matter of regret, however, throt the supply of pupils entering for the teaching profession is still below the average, notwithstanding the rapid extension of Training College accommodation and the greater Inducements offered to teachers by Education Com- mittees. In summing up the work of the school during the past session, the leading features are the increased attention paid to the interests of the girls and the organisation of the work in each department, so as to create a more vivid and living interest on the part of the pupils. Every healthy stimulus has been brought into play so as to develop the individuality and initiative of every pupil. In concluding this report, I wish to tender thanks to the Education Committee and the Director of Educa- tion for the generous provision of apparatus necessary for the successful %orking of the school, also to the parents, for the kind support which they have given to the teachers whose generous services, carried out some- times under trying conditions, have enabled me to develop a successful scheme of Secondary Education for Warrington. (Applause.)

div.head: MAYOR'S HINTS TO STUDENTS.
div.p: THE MAYOR'S HINTS TO STUDENTS.
_ The MAYOR, in an interesting address to the vholars, said that although be agreed with the Chair- mm that we ah.nld still move forward educationally,

he did not think it was always a good plan to make everything too easy. Something should be left to effort. His Worship made favourable comment on the fact that at the Secondary School the curriculum was such as to educate both the band and the eye, and he showed how manual dexterity also conduced to mental alertness. He next pointed the analogy between knowledge as applied to the brain and food as applied to the body. In the first instance, he said, the child was only capable of learning through imitation and later on through memory, but he would exhort even the comparatively young children to begin to use their thoughts and to try to understand what they were committing to memory. By that means they would remember it for an indefinite time. From the very first, he (the Mayor) had deducted for himself and things he learned in early boyhood he could still remember very well. Knowledge acquired by reading or learning was of comparatively no use unless it were thought over and improved by the mind after it had ben received. Giving hints on aids to the acquire- ment of knowledge, his Worship placed first the

ENCOURAGEMENT OF A. HAPPY FRAME OF MIND. There was no better way of doing that than by healthy exercise and by having a good feeling towards their companions and showing kindliness and humaneness towards the lower animals. Just as physical health aided the digestion of food, so the means he had mentioned aided the digestion and the acquirement of particles of knowledge. Music also improved the digestion Of food. At a large banquet an orchestra was generally set going to improve the appetite and the digestion of those partaking of the meal. In the same way, anything which gave rise to a pleasant frame of mind increaSed the power of the mind to acquire and retain knowledge. He believed that botany was a means of encouraging the powers of observation. They might not know the name of the stray flower which they plucked during their walks in the country, but they could dissect it, find out the arrangement of the petals and other organs, and refer it to its natural order. They could not exercise their good powers too early, so as to give:them a bent in the proper direction. It would boa gain in framing their future careers. Hero worship was an excitement of ambition and it also helped them in their choice of avocation. Under the heading of "hero worship," he would also place the advantage of paying respect to those of their seniors who had had superior experience. It was a fault of the young to strike out on a new line for themselves and not to defer suf`ici- ently to the advice of those who had gone over the ground before them. His Worship finally directed attention to the value of old proverbs, especially quot- ing buch sayings as' Virtue is its own reward," "Its's an ill wind that blows nobody good," and " The proof of the pudding is in the eating. Such proverbs were likely to prove a real guide to young people in later life. They were composed before there were any statistics to demonstrate the wisdom or futility of certain courses of action, but it was realised that in a large number of cases a certain thing happened and some observer, more acute than the rest, combined the results of their experiences in the form of proverbs. There was not a single one of them that could be challenged as incorrect. It might be a rather eccentric idea, but it had recently struck him that proverbs were very valuable guides to them as to what they should do or avoid. He was sorry be did not arrive at that conclusion earlier, for he might have avoided many errors he had committed. C.mncillor JENKINS proposed and Councillor BI RTLES seconded a vote of thanks to the Mayor and warmly eulogised his devoted and self-sacrificing efforts for the welfare of the town.

The vote was heartily passed. Mr. PLINbToN, in moving a vote of thanks to the Chairmtn. said Mr Jolley was more abused than many pe Iple for the simple reason that he had convictions as c%oll as thorough sincerity and, whether people differed from him or not, he always adhered to his policy. He (Mr Plinston) hid differed from Mr Jolley many times, but he was convinced that no man served the borough of Warrington more faithfully than Mr Jolley. (Applause).

div.head: SHORTAGE OF TEACHERS.
div.p: THE SHORTAGE OF TEACHERS.

1\ Ir. J. Moons: MURRAY", in seconding, said reference had been made to a possible scarcity of teachers. It was not a possible scarcity ; it was there already. They had had it for the past ten years. The only ground for the claim that there was an excessive surplus of teachers had been the fact that all teachers had come out of the training colleges at the same time and it had been extremely difficult to find them all places at once. Ile had recoros for the past ten years and it might surprise his hearers to know that while the Warington authority bad appointed on the average 39 teachers every year, they had only produced something like 18 teachers in Warrington, so that they had to get just as many from elsewhere. That was only indicative of the state of affairs throughout the country. Takiog the year through, they were always wanting teachers and the future before teachers was the very brightest that they had ever had to look forward to. Mr Murray referred to the disinclination on the part of many Warrington parents to allow their children to take up situations outside their native town and pointed out that promising youths were sometimes handicapped in that way. Last year the Warrington Education Committee had the power to nominate a 'candidate for the position of engineering artificer in the navy—a step on the ladder that aby could climb till he became engineer-in-chief. Yet the committee had some difficulty in finding candidates, because the selected boy would have to leave home. Parents should remember that their boys would have to be left souse time and they would have more confidence in leaving them if they knew they were fitted for the battle of life. He appealed to parents to look a little further than their own town,for there were say number of appointments open outside. (Applause). The vote was cordially passed.

div.head: ENTERTAINMENT.
div.p: THE ENTERTAINMENT.

The entertainment, for which the scholars were responsible, was most interesting and reflected great credit upon the school. The choir,under the conductor- ship of Mr J B Baxter, sang the choruses " Snow " (Elgar), " Spring is here ' (Teazle), " The Dawn of May " (Berger) and" Summer Song " (Barnby) in very pleasing style, tone, time and expression alike being good. Miss Alice Jarman played the pianoforte accompaniments. A scene from "Alice in Wonderland" was charmingly performed by Ella Cotton, Muriel Critchley and Lillie Weston, who took their parts very naturally and fully brought out the quaint humour of the work. The French play "La Poudre aux Yeux ":also proved highly amusing, the characters being sustained in admirable style by the following :—M. Ratinois, Thomas Cole ; M. Malingear, William Swaine ; M. Robert. oriole de Mdtue. Ratinois, John H Ball ; M. Fred6ric, flls de M. Ratinois, Sydney Parsonage; Le nhgre-domestique de M. Ratinois, John Foulkes; Mme. Ratinois, Grace Lees ; Mme. Malingear, Lilies Johnson ; Emmeline, fills de M. Malingear, Bessie Harter; Alexandrene, femme-de-chambre de Mme. Malingear, Eveline Butterworth ; Jos4phine, femnie-de-chambre de Mine. Ratinois, Dorothy McNeil; Sophie, cuisinilsre de Mme. Malingear, Esther Kilshaw. The stage properties were lent by the management of the Royal Court Theatre. The audience then adjourned to the school-yard where a number of scholars gave an exhibition of Morris dancing. They had been well trained and executed the old-world measures with delightful freedom and neatness. The visitors inspected with interest some examples of work done by the pupils in the various departments of the school.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Despite the very hot weather, large houses have assembled at the Hippodrome nightly and if patrons have been uncomfortable in a slight degree on account of the excessive heat they have been amply repaid, for tae programme submitted is of such a quality that one forgets the heat and enjoys the fare to the fullest extent. Ernest Krake appears with his company of clever commedians in an amusing comedy act "The electric tram conductor" in which some acrobatic feats are smartly introduced. There is an abundance of good comedy and the eccentric conductor's dealings with the various " fares " along with the many other amusing incidents, keep the audience in one continual roar of laughter. Louise Zetland is a dainty artiste with a good voice which she uses in an artistic man- ner. Her efforts during the week have received the unstinted applause of the delighted audiences. Spry and Monti appear in quite a new scene. "The erratic song writer " with a large amount of success, the humour being of that neat, witty type which pleases and entertains the audience from the commencement. The Lyons trio acquit themselves admirably in a pantomamic absurdity in which some good tumbling is introduced. In coon songs and dances Harry Raymond and Ivy gave us something entirely new in the terpsichorean art and their antics are well worthy of the large amount of praise showered upon them. In addition to being a very clever exponent of the art of ordinary step dancing Horace Horner astonishes and pleases with some difficult steps on a narrow board whilst balancing himself on his head. The Dennisons are a pleasing duo and give us an able rendition of a popular coon song. The harmonising in this song is well done and the house is unstinted in its applause. As lightning dancers they also "hit the mark." An eccentric funniosity indeed is Dan Whitlev. who gives three songs in a breezy and captivating way. His vocal efforts are interspersed with a host of new and witty gags which cannot fail to take. Lil Sprightly, character comedienne, is fairly successful in her studies and in addition two, excellent films are shown on the cenematograph. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. The famous Craggs in their latest comedy sketch "Billy" head a good bill for next week and they ar ably supported by S W Wyndham, comedian; Phil Kauffman, the popular coon; Arthur Astill, the , whistling ploughboy; Haleys garden of girls in vocal ' and dancing scena ; Lily &utter, characteristic ' comedienne; and Molly Sayers, comedienne.

There was RD interesting game between St Helens Cable Co, juniors and WeHeld, the former winning by 14 runs. Hill (11), Mather (0) and Watson (9) la`ted well for the winners. Forster, for Wel!field, captured seven wickets for 14 runs. For the Cable eleven Bowers took 4 wickets for 8 runs and Mather 3 wickets for 5 rune. Emmanuel Institute achieved a creditable victory over Penketh Friends' School, but there was nothing particularly notable about the play. J Ellison (14), J Palmer (12) made the most usetul efforts with the bat. Arley had to bow the knee to Lynam who amassed 74 and got all the visitors out for 32. The scoring was low, E Rose (15) being the most successful with the bat. Time robbed Winwick As3lum of a win on Saturday, when they entertained Manchester Linotype. Winwick knocked up a total of 172, and dismissed seven of the visitors for 122. Chief honours were carried off by C Cunningham (55), and G Floyd (46), and for the visitors by H Yates, who scored 33 and took four wickets for 46 runs.
